Memory Outlook – CITI

1. Memory Industry Outlook: Continued Decoupling of Premium and Conventional Memory

We expect that the ongoing decoupling between premium memory and conventional memory will persist in the memory industry as memory demand becomes increasingly concentrated on AI and server applications. As a result, memory suppliers are refraining from aggressive capital expenditure plans due to the long-term weakness of conventional memory. Instead, they are executing a cautious investment strategy focused on the expansion of advanced process nodes, which is expected to limit the increase in supply in 2025.
In the DRAM segment, suppliers are anticipated to expand front-end investments in 1b/1c nanometer processes to enhance the capabilities for HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) and AI DRAM. In the NAND segment, investments are expected to facilitate the transition from conventional processes to advanced NAND processes with over 200 layers. Amid limited supply, the DRAM market is projected to start its recovery from Q2 2025, and the NAND market from Q3 2025—earlier than the previously forecasted recovery of Q3 for DRAM and Q4 for NAND.

2. DRAM Market: Price Recovery Expected from Q2 2025
We anticipate that DRAM prices will begin a recovery phase from Q2 2025, driven by increased demand related to AI. This recovery will be supported by rising demand from AI-related HPC (High-Performance Computing) and on-device AI, net die loss due to HBM and DDR5, and the price premium of next-generation HBM products. Additionally, accelerated procurement activities and inventory normalization among data center customers—aimed at supporting the AI data center construction planned for 2026—are expected to strongly boost server DDR5 demand.

3. NAND Market: Slower Recovery Expected from Q3 2025
NAND prices are expected to recover starting in Q3 2025, but at a slower pace compared to the DRAM market. While the surge in AI-related demand is anticipated to drive DRAM recovery, the impact on additional demand creation in the NAND sector is relatively limited, leading to a more modest increase in demand.

4. DRAM and NAND Supply/Demand (S/D) Outlook
For the DRAM industry, the supply/demand ratio is projected to improve to -1.0% in 2025 and -1.2% in 2026, driven by increased demand from AI-related applications. We forecast global DRAM demand to grow by 15.0% and 19.2% year-over-year in 2025 and 2026 respectively, while supply is expected to increase by 13.9% and 19.2% over the same periods. Annually, the average selling price (ASP) for DRAM is expected to rise by 15.4% in 2025 and 20.4% in 2026.

In the NAND industry, the S/D ratio is anticipated to remain balanced at +0.3% in 2025, with a partial recovery in the eSSD segment, although other segments may continue to face challenging demand conditions. We expect NAND bit supply to increase by 9.8% and 34.3% year-over-year in 2025 and 2026 respectively, with bit demand growing by 9.4% and 36.7% respectively. On an annual basis, the NAND ASP is projected to decline by 6.3% in 2025 and 6.5% in 2026.

DS Investment & Securities – Recommends Samsung Electronics as the Top Pick for the Short Term

Review of the Rapidly Changing Memory Supply and Demand Situation

According to our channel checks, the inventory adjustment for mobile DRAM in China has nearly reached its final stage, and the spot prices for DDR4 are also rising, mainly centered on LPDDR4. It is assessed that CXMT’s supply cannot fully meet the demand for LPDDR4, which is predominantly installed in mid-to-low-end smartphones eligible for the Gu Hwan-shin subsidy.

For DDR5, memory companies had not maintained high inventory levels to begin with, and with the ongoing transition to HBM, supply has been declining. In China, orders for DDR5 used in high-performance PCs and servers are also seen to be increasing. Although there is a possibility that some orders were accelerated due to concerns over rising tariffs, it is expected that demand for server-grade DDR5 will further increase in the second half of the year.

Although NAND still has high inventory levels among customer companies and memory manufacturers (around a 10-week supply), channel checks indicate that Taiwanese module companies (Phison, ADATA, AVEXIR, JMicron) are increasing their order volumes. In the short term, they appear to be stockpiling inventory at lower prices amid production cuts, but purchases are expected to continue when actual demand rebounds in the second half.

While a clear signal of improved demand has not yet emerged, price increases are expected to persist in the first half of the year. The key factors now are whether demand increases in the second half and how quickly channel inventories are depleted. Although the increase in set demand for the latter half remains uncertain, it is clear that prices have entered an upward trend in the first half due to memory companies maintaining a conservative supply stance. The fact that supply has not expanded despite rising prices is further encouraging customer companies to accumulate inventory. The Micron earnings announcement on March 20 is expected to be an important milestone from a supply-demand perspective.

Samsung Electronics Recommended as the Top Pick in April – Continuous Monitoring of Demand Conditions Required

We maintain a buy recommendation for large-cap semiconductor stocks from March to April and recommend Samsung Electronics as our top pick until April. This comes at a time when expectations for a rise in memory prices are spreading. There is potential for upward revisions in the profit estimates of memory companies, and Samsung Electronics is expected to show a stronger profit recovery in general-purpose memory—particularly driven by increased sales of mid-to-low-end smartphones in China.

SK Hynix’s stock price increase is expected to be driven by an increase in server demand in the second half of the year.

It is necessary this year to continuously monitor the memory supply-demand situation and price trends while reviewing investment strategies. Even in March–April 2024, a steep rise in NAND prices was observed due to supply adjustments and eSSD inventory stockpiling, but prices fell again in the second half as supply expanded amid weak demand. This is also the reason for recommending a short-term investment strategy.

Semiconductor materials and components stocks had shown strong performance mainly among legacy companies over the past month, and recently, the entire sector has been on the rise. Since stock prices have risen reflecting expectations for price increases, it is believed that further gains will require strong earnings support. We still favor stocks with exposure to high-end DRAM and AI.

Citi) NVIDIA GTC2025 Review: Buy SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics

NVIDIA to Adopt 1TB HBM4e for Rubin 
Ultra

At NVIDIA’s GTC 2025 conference, detailed HBM specifications for its next-generation GPU platforms were unveiled. The Rubin Ultra platform notably adopts a 1TB HBM4e, significantly exceeding prior expectations, and offers 3.5 times more HBM capacity compared to Blackwell Ultra’s 288GB. NVIDIA announced Rubin Ultra would launch in the second half of 2027, following the Vera Rubin NVL144 platform, offering improved high-speed memory capacity of 75TB per rack (compared to Blackwell Ultra NVL72’s 40TB). Demand for 1TB HBM4e is expected to gain momentum from mid-2026, impacting the HBM market in 2026. NVIDIA also highlighted promising figures, projecting data center investments to reach $1 trillion by 2028, with 3.6 million Blackwell GPU orders anticipated from the top four U.S. hyperscalers in 2025 (compared to Hopper’s 1.3 million units).

Positive Market Impact for HBM Suppliers: Buy SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics

Driven by accelerated HBM content growth from NVIDIA’s next-gen platforms, we have increased confidence in sustained tight supply-demand dynamics for HBM through 2025 and beyond. Considering the HBM capacity growth outlined in NVIDIA’s roadmap, we believe HBM content growth will significantly impact future HBM demand outlooks. We maintain a constructive stance on robust HBM demand growth and prefer Korean HBM suppliers. Our top Buy recommendations are SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.

Samsung Electronics: Target Price KRW 83,000
Valuation:
The 12-month target price of KRW 83,000 for Samsung Electronics is derived using the sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) methodology based on 2025 projected EBITDA. For total enterprise value calculation, fair EV/EBITDA multiples were assigned to five key segments based on global peers: Memory (7.2x), Foundry (6.0x), Display Panel (3.2x), Mobile (7.5x), and Home Appliances (3.5x). These multiples align with relevant competitor trading multiples.
Risks:
Potential downside risks include: 1) longer-than-expected delays in HBM shipment approvals to major customers; 2) weaker-than-expected PC sales and disappointing NAND demand; 3) aggressive investments by competitors negatively affecting pricing in memory semiconductors/foundry; 4) intensified competition in the mobile market reducing Samsung’s mobile margins; 5) significant appreciation of the Korean won impacting Samsung’s earnings.

SK Hynix: Target Price KRW 350,000
Valuation:
The target price of KRW 350,000 for SK Hynix is derived by applying a 2.5x P/B multiple based on 2025 forecasts. This represents a 30% premium to the historical average P/B during periods of structural demand growth, reflecting our positive ASP outlook driven by robust premium memory demand growth and structural diversification of memory products due to customization and emerging AI memory demands.
Risks:
Potential downside risks for SK Hynix reaching the target price include: 1) decline in DRAM demand; 2) weaker-than-anticipated NAND demand; 3) global consumption collapse.

Report: NVIDIA Launches H20E, Requests HBM3E 8-Stack Supply from SK Hynix

According to reports from Korean media, SK Hynix recently received an additional supply request from NVIDIA for its HBM3E 8-stack product.

This order is intended for NVIDIA’s “H20,” which is positioned as a lower-cost AI accelerator.

Up to now, the H20 has been equipped with HBM3 (fourth-generation high-bandwidth memory) with a total capacity of 96GB. Due to its relatively lower computing performance, it did not adopt the latest HBM technology.

However, NVIDIA recently decided to equip the H20, slated for mass production in the first half of this year, with the HBM3E (fifth-generation) 8-stack product and has requested supply from SK Hynix. As a result, the total HBM memory capacity has increased to 144GB.

Because this is the first time HBM3E is being used in that product, it is reportedly referred to internally as “H20E.”

An industry insider well-versed in the matter stated, “NVIDIA recently placed an additional order with SK Hynix for HBM3E 8-stack products, and SK Hynix is busy responding. I understand that supply will begin as early as this month.”

Although the total supply volume has not been disclosed, the enhanced performance of the H20 is expected to expand SK Hynix’s HBM business more than initially anticipated. Previous industry estimates placed SK Hynix’s annual HBM supply to NVIDIA at around 9 billion gigabits (Gb). Taking this into account, supply could potentially reach around 10 billion Gb.

Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix Target Price Raised (Goldman Sachs)

1. DRAM Market Outlook

• In Q1, the decline in DRAM prices was smaller than initially expected (especially for server DRAM).

• Demand from Chinese server companies remains robust, and there have been observations of pre-buying for inventory accumulation due to concerns over tariffs.

• On the supply side, major players are operating conservatively with production increases as they adopt profit-driven strategies.

• Quality and yield issues among new entrants have resulted in a partial supply shortage.

• With an overall improvement in market sentiment, there is a possibility that the rebound in DRAM prices could occur earlier than the initially anticipated Q3.

• It is also projected that from Q2 onward, the rate of decline in DRAM contract prices will slow to the lower single digits and may even turn positive in Q3.

• Accordingly, the DRAM Total Addressable Market (TAM) in 2025 is expected to reach an all-time high of approximately $120 billion.

SK hynix Posts 158% Surge in 1Q Profit—Second-Highest on Record, HBM3E Propels It Ahead of Samsung

On April 24, South Korean semiconductor giant SK hynix reported its financial results for the first quarter of 2025, delivering a stellar performance driven by surging AI demand and pre-tariff inventory stocking by customers in the U.S. Revenue reached ₩17.6391T, up 41.9% YoY; operating profit soared 157.8% to ₩7.4405T; and net profit jumped 323% to ₩8.1082T—well above market expectations.

Both revenue and operating profit marked the second-highest levels in the company’s history, just behind the previous quarter. Operating margin rose by 1 percentage point to 42%, representing eight consecutive quarters of growth. Notably, SK hynix's first-quarter operating profit outpaced Samsung Electronics’ estimated ₩6.6T, extending its lead for a second straight quarter.

SK hynix attributed the strong performance during what is typically a seasonally slow period to robust demand from companies racing to build AI systems and stockpile inventory, which accelerated memory market growth beyond expectations. The company responded by ramping up sales of high-value products such as 12-layer HBM3E and DDR5.

As a key HBM supplier to NVIDIA, SK hynix expects continued growth in 12-layer HBM3E shipments in the second quarter, with the product projected to account for over 50% of total HBM3E revenue. The company reaffirmed its previous forecast that overall HBM demand in 2025 will double compared to last year.

TrendForce previously noted that the recent stockpiling surge has driven contract price increases for both DRAM and NAND Flash in Q2, exceeding earlier expectations. The ultimate direction of U.S. tariff policy remains the most critical factor for memory market supply-demand dynamics and pricing trends in the second half of the year.

Hanmi Semiconductor has maintained a close partnership with SK hynix since 2017, jointly developing thermal compression bonding (TC bonder) equipment. In 2024, Hanmi also began supplying this equipment to Micron, further expanding its client base. Notably, Hanwha Semitech, a rising competitor, is set to begin supplying TC bonders to SK hynix starting in 2025. This reflects a broader trend: as demand for HBM continues to rise, more equipment vendors are entering the TC bonder market, making the supply chain increasingly complex. HBM manufacturers are therefore actively seeking more diversified and resilient equipment supply networks.

As HBM chip stacking advances from 8hi to 12hi and 16hi configurations, TC bonders are required to meet higher performance standards, including greater alignment precision and adoption of fluxless processes. Established players like Hanmi, SEMES, and Shinkawa now face growing competition from newcomers such as Hanwha and ASMPT. The shifting market shares among these players will be worth watching closely.

TMT AI Ecosystem Meta-Analysis: Q1 2025 Earnings Insights

Executive Summary

The Q1 2025 earnings season provides compelling evidence that artificial intelligence remains the dominant secular growth driver across the technology ecosystem. Through careful analysis of key earnings transcripts released thus far, this report is a meta-analysis that identifies strategic inflection points, emerging trends, and investment opportunities across the AI value chain.

Several transformative themes have emerged:

AI infrastructure demand continues to outstrip supply, with hyperscalers, cloud providers, and a growing roster of enterprise customers competing for limited capacity.

Agentic AI represents the next major evolution, with forward-looking companies shifting from isolated use cases to comprehensive AI-led transformations focused on autonomous agents.

The AI inference opportunity is materializing faster than anticipated, driving meaningful demand for HBM memory, enterprise SSDs, and specialized accelerators.

Supply chain reconfiguration is accelerating amid tariff uncertainties, creating both challenges and opportunities for companies with manufacturing flexibility.

Power and environmental constraints are increasingly becoming the limiting factor for AI deployment, driving investment in specialized infrastructure.

AI Value Chain Analysis: Current Market Dynamics

Semiconductor Manufacturing & Equipment

ASML continues to benefit from AI-driven demand, maintaining its 2025 revenue outlook of €30-35 billion despite tariff uncertainties. EUV equipment remains crucial for advanced logic and memory production essential to AI systems. Management highlighted that AI remains "the key driver for growth" in the semiconductor industry, supporting their 2030 revenue target of €44-60 billion.

TSMC's AI-related business shows exceptional momentum, with management projecting AI accelerator revenue to double in 2025 and grow at a mid-40s percentage CAGR over the next five years. This trajectory supports TSMC's strategic investment in advanced manufacturing capacity, including an additional $100 billion investment in Arizona, bringing their total US commitment to $165 billion. Management specifically noted that AI reasoning models "will drive greater efficiency and help lower the barrier to future AI development."

SK Hynix has achieved leadership in DRAM as AI fundamentally transforms the memory market. Management emphasized that HBM is projected to grow at approximately 50% annually between 2024-2028, with HBM3E 12-high products set to comprise over half of HBM3E shipments in Q2. The company has also shipped the industry's first HBM4 samples, positioning them favorably for 2026 when HBM4 is expected to become the flagship product.

Intel is strategically refocusing its AI efforts under new CEO Lip Bu Tan, emphasizing three key emerging areas: reasoning models, agentic AI, and physical AI. The company has decided against building the previously announced Falcon Shores AI accelerator but maintains plans for Jaguar Shores. Management appears to be pivoting away from directly competing with NVIDIA in high-performance AI training accelerators to focus on edge AI, inference, and integrated full-stack solutions.

Cloud and Platform Services

Alphabet demonstrated impressive AI adoption metrics with AI Overviews reaching 1.5 billion monthly users. The introduction of AI Mode in Search, which management notes generates queries twice as long as traditional search queries, shows promising early results. The Gemini 2.5 model release represents a significant performance improvement that management describes as "widely recognized as the best model in the industry." Google Cloud revenue grew 28% to $12.3 billion, with management highlighting strong AI-driven demand.

ServiceNow reported exceptional performance in AI offerings with Pro Plus deals more than quadrupling year-over-year. Management emphasized their leadership in agentic AI through the Yokohama release, which introduced pre-packaged AI agents, an orchestration engine, and agent-to-agent communication capabilities. Their RaptorDB, positioned as "the next-generation database for the AI world," is seeing accelerating adoption.

Infosys highlighted a strategic shift in client AI approaches from isolated use cases to comprehensive AI-led transformations using AI agents. The company has developed 200+ AI agents deployed across industries and manages approximately 400 active AI projects. Management reported varying productivity benefits across domains, including 20-25% improvements in code development and 30-40% in customer service.

Data Center Infrastructure

Digital Realty achieved record pricing at $244 per kilowatt per month for new data center leasing (up 10% from their prior record), reflecting the significant impact of AI infrastructure on demand dynamics. The company reported strong leasing momentum with a record backlog of $919 million, providing visibility into 2026 and beyond. Management noted that demand is diversifying beyond traditional hyperscale and colocation providers to include "neocloud" providers and enterprise customers.

Vertiv delivered exceptionally strong results with 25% organic revenue growth and record backlog of $7.9 billion. Management highlighted robust demand for their liquid cooling solutions, which typically precede chip deployment by three to six months, making them a leading indicator of AI infrastructure build-out. Tariff mitigation strategies include supply chain reconfiguration and strategic pricing actions.

Energy & Power

GE Vernova characterized the current environment as an "electricity supercycle" driven by manufacturing growth, industrial electrification, EVs, and data center needs. Management described an "unprecedented need for investment" in power generation and grid infrastructure to support AI and digital transformation. Despite a $300-400 million estimated impact from tariffs, the company maintained its full-year guidance.

EQT Corporation is positioning to capitalize on expected growth in natural gas demand from data centers and AI, projecting up to 6-7 Bcf/day of local demand growth in Appalachia by 2030. Management noted that data center operators are seeking security of supply for their multi-billion dollar investments, creating opportunities for direct supply contracts with premium pricing.

Generative AI Commercial Adoption

A significant shift is occurring in enterprise AI strategy, with companies moving beyond experimental AI applications toward transformative business models built around generative AI and autonomous agents.

ServiceNow reported that the number of deals with three or more Now Assist AI products has quadrupled year-over-year, with average ACV deal sizes growing by one-third quarter-over-quarter. Management highlighted that customers are rapidly adopting their agentic AI capabilities, with pre-packaged AI agents for specific use cases deployable in just a few weeks.

Infosys revealed that generative AI has become an integral component of almost all deal discussions, representing a qualitative shift in how solutions are developed and delivered. The company reported working with a European client to implement AI as an enterprise-wide platform targeting up to 70% process improvements.

Alphabet noted that all 15 Google products with over half a billion users now incorporate Gemini models, demonstrating the mainstreaming of generative AI capabilities. Management emphasized that multimodal queries are growing significantly, with Circle to Search available on 250+ million devices and monthly visual searches increasing by 5 billion since October 2024.

Geographical Trends and Regulatory Impacts

Regional dynamics are evolving as companies navigate geopolitical tensions, tariffs, and differing rates of AI adoption:

North America continues to lead in AI infrastructure deployment, with TSMC noting approximately 60% of its gas turbine orders/slot reservations are in the US. Digital Realty reported that their strongest bookings in Q1 were in North America hyperscale, particularly in Northern Virginia. GE Vernova noted that about one-third of their 21GW in slot reservations is for data centers, expected to convert to orders in second half of 2025.

Europe is lagging in AI infrastructure build-out according to multiple companies. Vertiv noted that Europe lags other regions in AI adoption, though pipelines are encouraging. The company highlighted the iGenius project as an example of sovereign AI deployment in Europe, suggesting growing demand for independent AI capabilities. Digital Realty indicated that EMEA was their biggest "importer" with strong activity from all other regions.

Asia shows varying adoption patterns. SK Hynix reported strong performance in China and continued market growth in the rest of Asia, with India specifically mentioned as showing strength. TSMC's first specialty fab in Kumamoto, Japan started volume production in late 2024, with a second specialty fab to begin construction later this year.

Tariffs and trade policies emerged as a significant theme across multiple earnings calls. ASML noted increasing uncertainty due to evolving tariff discussions, while TSMC, Vertiv, Digital Realty, and GE Vernova all outlined mitigation strategies for tariff impacts. Management teams generally expressed confidence in their ability to navigate these challenges through supply chain reconfiguration, contractual provisions, and strategic pricing actions.

Memory & Storage Evolution: HBM and Enterprise SSDs

The AI infrastructure boom is driving unprecedented demand for specialized memory and storage solutions:

HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) continues to see extraordinary growth trajectories. SK Hynix management projects an average HBM growth rate of approximately 50% per year between 2024-2028. The company is transitioning to HBM3E 12-high products, which will comprise over half of their HBM3E shipments in Q2. First samples of HBM4 have shipped to major customers, with mass production preparation planned for completion within 2025.

Enterprise SSD demand is growing significantly, particularly for high-capacity models. SK Hynix achieved over 300% growth in enterprise SSD sales compared to 2023, leveraging their leadership in high-capacity QLC products. The high-capacity QLC enterprise SSD market is transitioning from 61TB in 2024 to 122TB in 2025, with development underway for 244TB products.

Both segments are experiencing pricing strength due to supply constraints and robust demand for AI workloads, with inference applications emerging as a major growth driver alongside training.

Agentic AI: The Next Frontier

A key insight from this earnings season is the accelerating shift toward agentic AI - autonomous, goal-directed systems that can execute complex workflows with minimal human intervention.

ServiceNow positioned itself as "leading the AI race" through their end-to-end agentic AI-first approach. Their Yokohama release introduced:
Pre-packaged AI agents for specific use cases
An orchestration engine for complex workflows
Studio tools for building custom agents
Agent-to-agent communication capabilities

Management noted that enterprises can deploy these AI agents in just a few weeks because they're pre-trained and understand specific use cases.

Infosys highlighted that clients are increasingly shifting from isolated AI use cases to comprehensive AI-led transformations using AI agents. The company has developed 200+ AI agents deployed with clients across multiple industries and is seeing productivity benefits ranging from 20-25% in code development to 30-40% in customer service.

Intel's strategic pivot includes a specific focus on "agentic AI" as one of their three key emerging areas. This suggests that even in the semiconductor space, there's recognition that the next wave of AI will be defined by autonomous, agent-based systems.

The rise of agentic AI represents a significant evolution beyond current generative AI capabilities, potentially creating new winners and losers as the market develops.

Supply Chain Reconfiguration and Tariff Impact

Tariff concerns emerged as a consistent theme across earnings calls, with companies implementing various mitigation strategies:

Vertiv detailed a comprehensive tariff mitigation strategy, explaining that its U.S. business is supplied through a mix of U.S. capacity, Mexico production (mostly USMCA qualified), and a small percentage from China and other regions. Management outlined mitigation actions including USMCA qualification for remaining Mexico supply chain, rebalancing toward low/no tariff regions, strategic production relocation, and targeted price actions.

GE Vernova estimated a $300-400 million impact from tariffs and resulting inflation. Management is responding with contractual provisions to pass through costs, supply chain relocation (two-thirds of China spend already dual-qualified elsewhere), and accelerated G&A cost transformation.

Digital Realty expects a modest (<5%) tariff impact due to US/Mexico/Canada-focused supply chains and proactive component ordering. Management highlighted their long-standing vendor relationships as providing supply chain advantages that differentiate them from other providers.

TSMC acknowledged that "under today's fragmented globalization environment, overseas fab costs are higher for everyone." The company's massive $165 billion investment in US manufacturing will reshape the US semiconductor ecosystem, though management noted that overseas fab expansion is expected to cause 2-3% gross margin dilution in 2025.

These supply chain reconfigurations are creating both challenges and opportunities across the technology ecosystem, with companies that have manufacturing flexibility and global footprints likely to outperform those with concentrated supply chains.

Investment Implications

Based on this comprehensive analysis of Q1 2025 earnings calls, several key investment themes emerge:

Specialized AI Infrastructure Providers demonstrating pricing power and supply constraints represent compelling opportunities. Companies like Vertiv and Digital Realty are benefiting from record pricing and strong backlog visibility while facing relatively manageable tariff impacts.

HBM Memory Leaders are positioned for sustained above-market growth. SK Hynix stands out with their leadership in HBM3E and early positioning in HBM4, supporting their projection of 50% annual growth through 2028.

Agentic AI Platform Providers are capturing increased enterprise spending as companies shift from experimental AI to transformation. ServiceNow's quadrupling of Pro Plus deals and Infosys's 200+ deployed AI agents highlight this trend.

Energy Infrastructure supporting the AI boom presents secular growth opportunities. GE Vernova's characterization of an "electricity supercycle" and EQT's projection of 6-7 Bcf/day of local demand growth from data centers by 2030 underscore this theme.

Companies with Supply Chain Flexibility are better positioned to navigate tariff uncertainties. Those with diverse manufacturing footprints and the ability to reconfigure supply chains quickly should command premium valuations in this environment.

Key Risks to Monitor

Several risks could impact the trajectory of AI-related investments:

Power Constraints may increasingly limit AI deployment, creating bottlenecks despite strong demand. Power availability and environmental considerations could become significant limiting factors.

Escalating Tariffs represent a growing uncertainty, with potential impacts on costs, margins, and demand. While companies are implementing mitigation strategies, further escalation could disrupt supply chains and pressure margins.

Hyperscaler Spending Patterns may introduce volatility. While management teams generally dismissed concerns about potential slowdowns, concentrated customer bases create inherent risks.

Model Efficiency Improvements could eventually moderate infrastructure requirements, though this appears to be offset by increasing model complexity and expanding use cases in the near term.

Valuation Expansion across AI-related sectors may limit further upside despite strong fundamentals. Many stocks already price in significant growth expectations.

Conclusion: Strategic Positioning

The Q1 2025 earnings season reveals an AI ecosystem that continues to accelerate and evolve, with particular momentum in infrastructure, agentic AI, and inference applications. Companies at the nexus of these trends with strong execution capabilities appear best positioned for outperformance.

The most compelling investment opportunities exist in:

AI Infrastructure - Companies enabling the physical deployment of AI systems with pricing power and visibility
Memory & Storage - Specialized providers supporting the unique requirements of AI workloads
Agentic AI Platforms - Solutions that enable enterprises to deploy autonomous, goal-directed AI systems
Energy Infrastructure - Power and cooling systems that address the fundamental constraints on AI deployment

While headline risks around tariffs and potential hyperscaler spending fluctuations warrant monitoring, the underlying secular growth trend in AI remains intact and continues to create significant investment opportunities across the technology ecosystem.

$NVDA $AMD Channel checks across more than 50 industry contacts indicate that underlying demand for accelerator GPUs remains exceptionally robust, with reported unit or dollar growth of 10‑50 % year‑over‑year driven almost entirely by generative‑AI inference roll‑outs and the continued build‑out of training clusters. Lead times for high‑end NVIDIA parts are still quoted at 9‑18 months and, despite isolated anecdotes of improved availability, most hyperscalers and enterprise VARs describe persistent allocation, especially on networking cards and HBM‑attached SKUs. The structural driver remains the widening gap between conventional CPU performance and the compute and memory‑bandwidth requirements of large language models, which is forcing virtually every new AI workload to deploy on a GPU or an ASIC that copies the NVIDIA programming model.

Pricing dynamics are bifurcating sharply. Street‑level quotes for the current‑generation H100 have started to compress by 5‑20 % as AMD’s MI300A/X family enters volume and some channel partners seek to clear inventory ahead of Blackwell. By contrast, forward contracts for Blackwell GB200 blades, particularly the NVL72 racks, are closing at a meaningful premium to H100—often list or better—because hyperscalers value the node‑count reduction and energy savings the new architecture delivers. Enterprises without deep AI engineering talent are willing to trade price for access to performance per watt, leading to a two‑tier market in which trailing silicon commoditises quickly while bleeding‑edge SKUs remain supply‑constrained and margin‑rich. Importantly, several contacts highlighted intensifying price sensitivity in cloud GPU rentals; that is likely to force public cloud providers either to accept lower margins or to migrate more rapidly toward internally designed accelerators.

On the supply side, the real bottleneck is shifting from GPU die output to the memory and power infrastructure that surrounds the silicon. HBM3E capacity at both Samsung and Micron is effectively sold out through at least calendar Q4 and the incremental expansion of TSV lines is gating volume for every vendor, including AMD. Power‑delivery constraints inside new data‑centre builds are also starting to cap near‑term rack deployments; multiple cloud architects cite substation delays of up to 18 months as the critical path rather than board availability. That dynamic favours vertically integrated players such as Microsoft and Alphabet that can secure incremental megawatts and reinforces the scarcity value of any chip that can deliver higher performance per watt—again underscoring why Blackwell and MI300X pricing is proving so resilient.

Performance interviews show that memory‑bandwidth, not raw FLOPs, is now the dominant purchase criterion. AMD is leveraging its Infinity Architecture and superior HBM bandwidth to win inference‑heavy workloads where latency matters more than absolute training throughput, while NVIDIA retains a decisive advantage in scaled training jobs thanks to its mature software stack and NVLink‑enabled cluster architecture. The widening focus on energy efficiency per token trained is stimulating interest in custom silicon, but timelines for most first‑party ASICs remain 2026+. Consequently, the established GPU incumbents should enjoy at least 6‑8 more quarters of outsized gross‑profit capture before meaningful disintermediation risk appears.

Competitive share trends reveal that AMD has pushed to roughly 40 % of data‑centre CPU shipments and is closing the gap in AI accelerators faster than expected, primarily by pricing aggressively and exploiting NVIDIA’s allocation constraints. Intel’s Gaudi roadmap is failing to resonate; its server CPU share has collapsed from 95 % to roughly 55 % over the last half‑decade and our contacts see no catalyst for reversal. Despite headline share erosion, NVIDIA still commands 90‑92 % of installed AI training capacity and, given two successive architecture wins (Hopper then Blackwell), is positioned to hold the lion’s share of training workloads through at least 2025. In networking, Broadcom’s dominance in switch ASICs persists, but early demand for NVIDIA’s Spectrum‑X Ethernet portfolio is emerging as the first credible threat in years; Marvell is seeing traction mainly where hyperscalers want custom silicon over merchant parts.

Investment implications are multifaceted. For NVIDIA, the data confirm that unit demand and mix are both skewing to higher‑ASP, higher‑margin products, providing clear earnings‑per‑share upside versus current sell‑side models that already assume mid‑teens sequential revenue growth into FY26; the key risk is whether power and HBM constraints cap shipment volumes below order books. For AMD, each percentage‑point of incremental accelerator share could translate to roughly USD 600‑800 M of annualised revenue given prevailing ASPs; however, sustainability depends on its ability to move to an annual cadence and secure enough HBM, which remains uncertain. Intel remains structurally challenged; without a competitive accelerator and with Sapphire Rapids yields still lagging, the company faces further gross‑margin compression and share loss, suggesting any long thesis must hinge on foundry optionality rather than product strength. Memory vendors Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron are positioned for outsized pricing power and margin expansion as HBM3E drags up blended DRAM ASPs; Micron, with the smallest installed DRAM base but fastest HBM ramp, offers the highest operating‑leverage torque. Broadcom’s switch ASIC franchise should continue compounding at mid‑teens with limited risk in the next 4‑6 quarters, but investors must monitor NVIDIA’s Ethernet attach as a potential headwind to 2026 growth. Finally, data‑centre REITs and power‑infrastructure suppliers may become critical ancillary beneficiaries, yet the long lead‑time nature of substation capacity injects a timing mismatch that could temper near‑term capital returns.

From a portfolio‑construction perspective, the read‑through argues for maintaining an overweight NVIDIA core position while opportunistically adding AMD on supply‑related pullbacks, pairing both against an underweight Intel. Layering in a long Micron or SK Hynix position hedges against any GPU unit volatility, as HBM scarcity should support memory margins even in a slower server upgrade cycle. Alpha generation will likely pivot on monitoring two variables: the pace at which Blackwell ramps relative to MI300X and any sign that hyperscale budgets rotate from GPUs toward internally developed ASICs sooner than 2026.

$MU $NVDA $TSM $VRT Micron’s guidance revision is unambiguously constructive for the generative AI infrastructure cycle and, importantly, it is pricing-led. For FQ4’25 (quarter ending 8/28/25), Micron raised revenue to $11.2B ±$0.1B from $10.7B ±$0.3B, lifted non‑GAAP gross margin to 44.5% ±0.5% from 42.0% ±1.0%, and took non‑GAAP EPS to $2.85 ±$0.07 from $2.50 ±$0.15, while tightening ranges. The midpoint raises imply +$0.5B revenue (+4.7%) and +2.5 ppts of gross margin vs prior guidance, with non‑GAAP opex nudged to $1.22B ±$0.015B from $1.20B ±$0.02B. Management explicitly attributes the revision to better pricing, particularly in DRAM, and strong execution. In other words, this is not a “one‑customer pull‑in” story; it reads as broad memory pricing strength in the quarter. (Micron Technology, Reuters)

Context strengthens the signal. Micron entered the quarter with HBM effectively sold out for CY25 and with HBM pricing largely pre‑determined, so an in‑quarter beat from “improved DRAM pricing” most likely reflects firmer conventional DRAM (server DDR5, mobile LPDDR5X, graphics GDDR) layered on top of locked‑in HBM volume. That is consistent with Micron’s June commentary that HBM revenue was inflecting and with 3rd‑party models that peg FY25 HBM revenue around $6B. The through‑line is that the AI compute buildout remains robust enough to tighten memory markets beyond HBM. (Micron Technology, Morningstar)

Demand drivers remain extraordinary and increasingly memory‑intensive. Hyperscaler capex is still stepping up: Microsoft has repeatedly telegraphed ~$80B of FY25 AI data center investment, Alphabet raised 2025 capex to roughly $85B, and Meta narrowed 2025 capex to $66–72B, explicitly citing GenAI scaling. On the deployment side, NVIDIA’s Blackwell platforms structurally raise memory content per accelerator: a DGX B200 node advertises 1.44 TB of HBM across 8 GPUs, and an NVL72 rack domain lists up to 13.4 TB of HBM3E; Blackwell Ultra B300 pushes to 288 GB HBM3E per GPU. Rising HBM per GPU, plus larger NVLink domains, translate directly into more bits per rack and higher memory dollar content per rack—even before you consider conventional DRAM on host CPUs. This is exactly the kind of mix shift that supports Micron’s pricing‑led upside. (The Official Microsoft Blog, Seeking Alpha, Meta, NVIDIA, Tom's Hardware)

Supply remains the swing factor, and the latest data points cut in favor of continued tightness through 2H25. TSMC’s CoWoS advanced‑packaging capacity, a known bottleneck for GPU+HBM systems, is expanding materially in 2025 toward ~60–75k wafers/month, which helps system availability but also enables HBM attachment to scale without flooding supply. Meanwhile, competitive dynamics in HBM continue to concentrate near‑term share at SK hynix and Micron; reports of Samsung’s slower 12‑Hi HBM3E qualification have persisted into mid‑2025, even as Samsung works to catch up. SK hynix, for its part, now frames AI memory TAM growth at ~30% CAGR to 2030, reinforcing a multi‑year runway for HBM and adjacent memory. The net is that 2H25 capacity relief is real at the packaging layer, but HBM stacking and validation remain the scarcer assets—supportive of price/mix and of Micron’s updated guide. (DIGITIMES Asia, TrendForce, Reuters)

Near‑term price action corroborates the thesis. Independent trackers flag sharp 3Q25 price increases for several DRAM categories as suppliers reallocate legacy capacity toward server and HBM. TrendForce has flagged double‑digit sequential moves in DDR4 and graphics DRAM and a 15–20% lift in HBM pricing into 3Q25. NAND is firming but less acute, with enterprise SSD contract pricing modeled up ~5–10% in 3Q25. Micron’s guidance revision lands squarely in this environment of tightening memory supply and rising DRAM ASPs. (Tom's Hardware, TrendForce)

For the broader generative AI infrastructure ecosystem, there are 6 investable implications. First, the profit pool is shifting incrementally toward memory through at least the Blackwell ramp. GPU BOMs are increasingly memory‑heavy and, while NVIDIA retains substantial pricing power, higher HBM and DRAM costs either compress accelerator margins or pass through into higher system ASPs. Given sustained demand elasticity in training capacity, we do not expect meaningful order deferrals; however, we do expect a rising memory share of rack‑level spend in 2H25–1H26, which accrues to HBM suppliers and to those with advantaged power/performance (e.g., Micron’s 12‑Hi 36 GB HBM3E). (Micron Technology)

Second, this update reduces the probability that memory availability will be the gating factor for Blackwell deployments in 4Q25–1H26; packaging and power look like the tighter constraints. NVIDIA itself underscores the power density of NVL72‑class racks, and supply chain checks continue to emphasize liquid cooling and power delivery as critical path items. That tilts incremental alpha toward data center power and thermal names with validated NVL72/GB300 reference designs, as well as optical interconnect suppliers riding the 800G→1.6T transition. (TrendForce, PR Newswire, Cignal AI)

Third, advanced packaging scarcity is easing but still strategic. As CoWoS output rises, substrate and interposer ecosystems remain tight but investable. TSMC’s step‑up through 2025 supports GPU+HBM shipments and should translate into continued backlog burn for substrate houses and organic RDL suppliers tied to CoWoS‑L and NVLink domains. We would fade the idea that packaging bottlenecks will structurally cap 2025 volumes; the bigger swing now is how quickly HBM 12‑Hi yields normalize at each DRAM vendor. (TrendForce)

Fourth, optics/networking remains a secular beneficiary rather than a budget casualty. Even with memory inflation, total AI rack budgets are expanding, not contracting, and 800G shipments are re‑accelerating with early 1.6T programs entering select deployments tied to Blackwell. The mix shift to larger NVLink or Ethernet memory‑coherent domains sustains switch ASIC, optical module, and NIC growth. We maintain an overweight stance on suppliers levered to 800G and early 1.6T ramps. (Cignal AI, https://t.co/wctbcPCigO)

Fifth, storage tightness is emerging but is secondary to DRAM. Enterprise SSD pricing is trending up mid‑single to low‑double digits into 3Q25, a modest headwind to AI factory TCO but not enough to alter deployment trajectories. The bigger architecture shift to watch is the industry’s exploration of tiered memory, including “high‑bandwidth flash” concepts that could augment HBM with stacked NAND for inference at lower cost/bit; these are longer‑dated (earliest 2027) and do not change 2025–2026 dynamics. (TrendForce, Tom's Hardware)

Sixth, policy is a 2026 risk rather than a 2025 blocker. The latest tariff rhetoric—100% chip tariffs on some imports with exemptions for companies manufacturing in the U.S., and separate arrangements with South Korea mitigating disadvantages—adds uncertainty to 2026 supply chains and pricing but has not derailed current AI memory flows. We treat it as volatility fuel rather than base‑case disruption for 2H25. (Reuters)

Investment implications are clear. For memory, the guidance lift validates a pricing and mix tailwind into the Blackwell ramp. We would add on weakness to high‑quality HBM‑levered names with proven 12‑Hi roadmaps and sold‑out 2025 books. In Micron’s case, the combination of a ~$0.5B revenue uplift, +2.5 ppts gross margin, and +14% EPS raise on pricing strength argues for upward estimate revisions into FY26 and supports the view that memory suppliers will take a larger slice of AI economics near term. The primary risk is 2026 HBM price normalization if TSV capacity and 12‑Hi yields overshoot demand; several watchers already flag double‑digit HBM price decline risk next year. We would manage this by trimming exposure as order books fill and by rotating into NAND‑heavy franchises or diversified memory names with 1‑gamma cost downs that can defend margins in a down‑ASP tape. (TrendForce)

For accelerators, the takeaway is slightly mixed but net positive. Strong memory pricing points to a healthy GPU pipeline, and CoWoS expansions reduce the chance that packaging caps shipments; however, BOM inflation from HBM can pressure accelerator margins at the margin if list prices are held flat into large pre‑negotiated CSP contracts. Given demand intensity, we still expect pass‑through to hold, but we would watch for scattered signs of CSPs optimizing configs (e.g., deferring 12‑Hi adoption in some inference footprints or mixing HBM capacities across racks) if HBM pricing stays at the top of the guided range. (TrendForce)

For data center power, cooling, and optics, the signal remains “go.” If memory is not the gating factor for 4Q25, the bottlenecks revert to power availability, liquid cooling, optics, and integration, all of which still show order strength. Names with validated NVL72/GB300 reference designs, liquid cooling IP, and 800G/1.6T exposure should continue to print above‑trend orders; the guidance shift from Micron reduces the tail risk of AI rack pushouts due to memory shortages. (https://t.co/2HXajdJv8P, Cignal AI)

Bottom line for the IC: Micron’s pricing‑driven guide raise is a high‑quality confirmation that AI memory remains the tightest, most value‑accretive component of the AI rack in 2H25. We would keep memory and advanced‑packaging beneficiaries as core longs through the Blackwell ramp, pair them against more consumer‑exposed DRAM names vulnerable to DDR4 price spikes, and lean into power/cooling and 800G optics as the next‑order constraints that convert directly into revenue. We would also start pre‑positioning for 2026 HBM price normalization risk by favoring suppliers with clear HBM4 transition plans, cost‑down nodes (1‑gamma), and balanced mix across DRAM and NAND so that gross margin resilience survives the inevitable ASP giveback. (GlobeNewswire)

$NVDA $AMD $AVGO $INTC The roadmap shows that the performance race in data‑center AI silicon is now primarily a packaging and memory race. Across 2025‑2028, the center of gravity shifts from monolithic silicon interposers (CoWoS‑S) to RDL‑based organic interposers with embedded silicon bridges (CoWoS‑L) for the highest‑end parts, while cost‑optimized designs adopt RDL interposers without large silicon (CoWoS‑R). That shift is driven by the need to exceed 3.3× reticle‑size packages, add more HBM stacks, and reduce the yield risk and cost of massive interposers. TSMC’s own technical disclosures set the guardrails: CoWoS‑S supports up to 3.3× reticle (~2,700 mm²) with deep trench capacitors (eDTC) in silicon, CoWoS‑R delivers 2/2 µm RDL on organic interposers, and CoWoS‑L combines wide‑pitch RDL with embedded Local Silicon Interconnect (LSI) that restores sub‑micron routing density and allows embedded eDTC under logic dies; TSMC began CoWoS‑L volume in 2024. For workloads that want even more HBM, TSMC has publicly discussed moving from 3.3× to 5.5× reticle packages with up to 12 HBM stacks in 2025‑2026 and targeting 9× reticle by 2027. The net implication is clear: package size, interconnect density, and power delivery—not just transistor count—are the limiting factors for next‑gen AI systems. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC, TrendForce)

Reading the roadmap by brand, the pattern is consistent with those technical constraints. NVIDIA’s H200 stays on CoWoS‑S with 141 GB of HBM3E, while Blackwell B200/GB200 move to CoWoS‑L with 192 GB of HBM3E, reflecting a package architecture change aimed at larger die complexes and more memory per GPU. AMD’s MI325X shipped with 256 GB, and the MI350 series is positioned at 288 GB HBM3E; both are CoWoS‑S today, with MI350 on newer process nodes and Micron publicly confirmed as a 12‑high HBM3E supplier to that platform. Intel’s Gaudi 3, fabbed on TSMC N5, uses 128 GB of HBM2E and remains on CoWoS‑S. Google’s Trillium/TPU v6e doubles HBM capacity and bandwidth versus v5e, also consistent with CoWoS‑class integration. Microsoft’s Maia 100 uses CoWoS‑S with 64 GB of HBM2E, explicitly trading to a less supply‑constrained HBM generation. Amazon’s Trainium2 advertises 96 GB HBM3E; credible industry reporting and disclosures describe a dual‑chiplet die with 4 HBM stacks on CoWoS‑S/R, which matches the “CoWoS‑R” callout in the chart. Meta’s MTIA 2 targets inference and uses 128 GB of LPDDR5 instead of HBM, a deliberate cost/power choice. These public facts substantiate the broad directions in the chart while reminding us that some rows (e.g., far‑future NVIDIA “VR”/“Feynman” and several 2027‑2028 entries) are directional rather than confirmed. (NVIDIA, Wccftech, AMD, Micron Technology, Intel CDRD, Google Cloud, ServeTheHome, Amazon Web Services, Inc., Meta AI)

Two supply bottlenecks dominate the investable landscape: CoWoS capacity and HBM supply. TSMC’s CoWoS output roughly doubled in 2024 and is on track to expand again in 2025; multiple industry trackers see 2025 monthly capacity in the 65k‑75k wafers range with further growth into 2026, yet demand still exceeds supply and pricing for CoWoS has risen by 10‑20%. On the memory side, SK hynix has had the volume and technical lead in HBM3/HBM3E, Micron is rapidly gaining share with 12‑high HBM3E and targets 20‑25% share, and Samsung is working to re‑establish leadership as HBM4 approaches. The price environment remains firm: several trackers have called out rising DRAM/HBM pricing into 2025, and HBM’s share of DRAM value is climbing into double digits. GPU sellers cannot ship without both CoWoS capacity and qualified HBM, which keeps the supply chain tight and shifts value capture upstream. (TrendForce, Micron Technology, Barron's)

How CoWoS‑S is built. CoWoS stands for chip‑on‑wafer‑on‑substrate. In CoWoS‑S, TSMC fabricates a passive silicon interposer (often on mature nodes like 65/55 nm) with TSVs and fine‑pitch BEOL routing, and integrates deep trench capacitors into the interposer to stiffen the power‑delivery network. Known‑good logic dies and HBM stacks are flip‑chip attached to the interposer at wafer scale, underfilled, and molded; after wafer‑level assembly the system is diced and mounted to an ABF organic substrate for board‑level attach and test. Critical materials and tools include copper plating and RDL patterning (Applied Materials Raider/Nokota, Lam’s SABRE and wet cleans), photosensitive polyimides and PBO dielectrics for RDL (HD Microsystems and peers), capillary and molded underfills (Namics; MR‑MUF is a well‑documented HBM process advantage at SK hynix), and temporary bonding/debonding and wafer handling systems for 2.5D/3D stacks (EV Group). Substrates use Ajinomoto Build‑up Film dielectric and are supplied by Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, Kinsus, and others. CoWoS‑S is the density and signal‑integrity leader, but massive interposers require reticle stitching, carry high mask cost, face bow/warpage risks, and hit practical limits around 3.3× reticle unless yields are exceptionally high. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, Applied Materials, Lam Research, HD Microsystems, Namics Corporation, Ajinomoto, Yahoo Finance)

How CoWoS‑R is built. CoWoS‑R deletes the giant silicon interposer and replaces it with an organic “RDL interposer” built up in polymer with multiple copper RDL layers. TSMC specifies 4 µm minimum pitch (2/2 µm L/S) and describes shielded ground‑signal stackups for high‑speed signaling. Because polymer has a lower modulus and different CTE, the RDL interposer acts as a mechanical buffer that reduces C4 bump strain energy density and improves reliability, and the RC of copper in polymer can be competitive at high frequencies. The tradeoff is lower routing density versus silicon and the inability to integrate on‑interposer eDTCs, which pushes more decoupling into the substrate or discrete components. CoWoS‑R improves cost and yield at large die sizes, which is why it appears on cost‑sensitive or moderately scaled parts like Trainium2. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC Research, Semiconductor Engineering)

How CoWoS‑L is built. CoWoS‑L marries a wide‑pitch organic RDL interposer with embedded LSI “bridge” dice in the areas that need ultra‑dense die‑to‑die links. Those LSI islands bring sub‑micron copper lines and TSV access back into the structure and can also embed eDTC blocks under logic dies. The result is a reconstituted interposer that scales beyond 3.3× reticle, supports more HBM stacks with short high‑density links where needed, and improves cost/yield because the high‑value silicon is confined to small bridges rather than a dinner‑plate‑sized interposer. TSMC has said CoWoS‑L entered volume in 2024 and has since mapped a path to 5.5× and 9× reticle packages with 12 HBM stacks, which aligns with Blackwell’s migration to CoWoS‑L. Intel’s EMIB and Samsung’s I‑CubeE are broadly analogous “embedded bridge + organic RDL” approaches available outside TSMC. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC, TrendForce, Intel, Samsung Semiconductor Global)

Manufacturers and who supplies what. Logic and bridges are overwhelmingly fabbed at TSMC for the chips on this roadmap, with Gaudi 3, NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell, AMD MI3xx/MI350, Google TPU v6, and Microsoft Maia all using TSMC nodes. Packaging for those parts is TSMC 3DFabric CoWoS in Taiwan; TSMC is also localizing a small portion of advanced packaging with Amkor in Arizona for U.S. supply‑chain resiliency later in the decade. Samsung Foundry offers I‑Cube and X‑Cube as alternatives, and Intel Foundry Services offers EMIB and Foveros, which are strategically important where customers want non‑TSMC supply. HBM stacks come from SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron; SK hynix currently leads, Micron is guiding to 20‑25% share and has confirmed design‑ins on AMD MI350, and Samsung is expected to re‑accelerate with HBM4. ABF substrates and build‑up dielectrics center on Ajinomoto’s ABF material; substrate suppliers with exposure to AI accelerators include Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, and Kinsus. Key equipment for CoWoS and HBM stacking includes copper ECD plating and wet cleans (Applied Materials, Lam), metrology/inspection (KLA, others), bonding/debonding and hybrid bonding for future HBM4/SoIC (EV Group, BESI), and underfill/encapsulants (Namics), along with polyimide/PBO dielectrics for RDL (HD Microsystems). (Intel CDRD, Amkor Technology, Samsung Semiconductor Global, Intel)

What this means brand by brand in 2025‑2027. For NVIDIA, CoWoS‑L is a risk and an opportunity. It is a necessary step to scale HBM count, package size, and bandwidth, but it introduces new yield and process‑integration variables versus the mature CoWoS‑S flow. Success depends on TSMC’s CoWoS‑L ramp and SK hynix/Micron/Samsung’s ability to supply HBM3E at 8‑high and 12‑high with acceptable thermals; tight CoWoS and HBM supply supports continued pricing power on Blackwell systems. For AMD, MI350 on CoWoS‑S should benefit from a stable process, larger HBM footprints, and Micron’s 12‑high HBM3E shipments; the main gating item is allocation of TSMC CoWoS and HBM supply. For Intel, Gaudi 3’s 128 GB HBM2E simplifies memory supply but risks losing on absolute bandwidth versus HBM3E/4 designs; it is priced to compete and leverages mature packaging. For Google and Microsoft, using CoWoS‑S with v6e and Maia 100 avoids the bleeding edge of CoWoS‑L and HBM3E qualification and has been explicitly framed as a TCO‑first design choice. For Amazon, Trainium2’s likely CoWoS‑R architecture suggests a deliberate cost/yield trade while still accessing HBM3E. For Meta, LPDDR5 keeps cost and power low for recommendation workloads while avoiding HBM entirely. The through‑line is that packaging choice is now a strategic lever for cost, yield, and time‑to‑ramp. (NVIDIA, Wccftech, Micron Technology, Intel CDRD, ServeTheHome, Amazon Web Services, Inc., Google Cloud)

The manufacturing playbook and where the bottlenecks live. In CoWoS‑S, the silicon interposer is processed with TSVs and multiple BEOL layers, HBM cubes are stacked by the memory vendors and delivered as known‑good stacks, then logic and HBM are micro‑bumped to the interposer with underfill and molding at wafer scale, followed by singulation and mount on ABF substrates. In CoWoS‑R, the interposer is reconstructed in polymer RDL on a carrier with multiple Cu layers and then assembled similarly. In CoWoS‑L, RDL build‑up proceeds, then LSI bridges are embedded in precise windows to deliver sub‑micron wiring only where needed, and eDTC blocks can be placed under logic dies to stabilize power delivery. The mechanical buffer properties of polymer and the lower RC of RDL at high frequency favor CoWoS‑R/L reliability, but organic RDL cannot match silicon interposer routing density; that is why bridges are necessary. Process control is non‑trivial for die warpage, coplanarity, and alignment in large packages; high‑throughput copper ECD, photosensitive polyimide RDL dielectrics, temporary wafer bonding/debonding, advanced underfill, and metrology are the scarce tools and materials. Those steps, not just the front‑end wafer fabs, are what gate shipments. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC Research, Applied Materials, Lam Research, HD Microsystems, https://t.co/IprQfflBAf)

Investment implications for the portfolio. First, TSMC remains the single biggest beneficiary of AI accelerator growth because it captures value in both wafers and advanced packaging. The company more than doubled CoWoS capacity in 2024, is expanding again in 2025, and is raising CoWoS prices by 10‑20% as demand outstrips supply; its plan to scale to 5.5× and eventually 9× reticle packages reinforces a multi‑year packaging moat. The most straightforward expression is to overweight TSMC against cyclic noise in handsets/PCs, with the risk that any CoWoS‑L yield hiccup or geopolitical shock disrupts shipments. Second, HBM suppliers are structurally advantaged. SK hynix holds the technology lead and the largest NVIDIA wallet share; Micron has secured AMD MI350 with 12‑high HBM3E and targets 20‑25% market share by 2025; Samsung’s near‑term risk is credibility on HBM3E quality but HBM4 is a re‑set opportunity. A barbell of SK hynix for leadership plus Micron for share gains is justified; underweight Samsung near term if evidence of qualification delays persists, with optionality to add on HBM4 progress. Third, ABF substrate suppliers are leveraged to the “bigger package” trend. Ajinomoto’s ABF resin is the de facto standard, while Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, AT&S, and Kinsus are the substrate names with increasing high‑end mix; Ibiden is expanding capacity specifically for AI, and yield differentials versus peers matter. A basket approach can work given single‑name volatility and customer concentration. Fourth, OSAT and localized packaging are investable as de‑risking plays. Amkor’s Arizona plant agreement with TSMC creates a long‑dated U.S. advanced‑packaging option; the financial impact is back‑loaded but the strategic value is significant for domestic supply chains. Fifth, equipment and materials are secular winners. Applied Materials and Lam Research monetise copper ECD, cleans, and packaging‑class wet processing for RDL and Cu pillars; EV Group and BESI are leveraged to temporary bonding and the coming wave of hybrid bonding in HBM4 and SoIC; Namics benefits from molded/board underfills in HBM stacks; KLA benefits from metrology/inspection of advanced packages. These exposures carry lower headline risk than a single GPU vendor while capturing the capex flywheel. (TrendForce, Yahoo Finance, Amkor Technology, Applied Materials, Lam Research, https://t.co/IprQfflBAf)

Risk disclosures and what to monitor. CoWoS‑L yield and module reliability are the largest near‑term unknowns because they introduce new failure modes relative to CoWoS‑S; watch TSMC’s OIP and customer ramp commentary. HBM availability will stay tight through 2025; any stumble by a key supplier can materially constrain shipments. DRAM price volatility and policy risk (export controls, tariffs) can affect HBM procurement and margins; the pricing bias for DRAM and HBM into 2025 remains upward. Substrate yields and lead‑times are a tactical risk, especially for very large designs moving toward 5.5× reticle packages; substrate scaling and glass‑core initiatives could be a 2026‑2027 wildcard. Finally, packaging competition exists: Intel EMIB‑M/T and Samsung I‑CubeE provide non‑TSMC heterogenous integration options, and large CSPs could dual‑source packaging to diversify risk. We would size positions with these execution and policy risks in mind, and continuously re‑underwrite allocation as evidence accumulates that CoWoS‑L and HBM4 ramp on schedule. (TrendForce, Intel, Samsung Semiconductor Global)

Technical appendix on CoWoS types for committee review. CoWoS‑S is the canonical 2.5D flow: large silicon interposer with TSVs and fine BEOL, 3.3× reticle limit, on‑interposer eDTC, best‑in‑class density/latency/PDN, and highest cost and mask count. CoWoS‑R is an organic RDL interposer with 2/2 µm wiring and multiple Cu layers, better mechanical compliance and reliability at scale, but lower density and no interposer eDTC; think Trainium‑class parts or mid‑range HBM footprints. CoWoS‑L embeds small LSI bridges within an RDL interposer, regaining sub‑micron routing exactly where needed and enabling embedded eDTC under logic; it scales beyond 3.3× to 5.5× and 9× reticle, enabling 12 HBM stacks for 2026‑2027 designs. Intel’s EMIB family performs the same functional role as LSI bridges inside an advanced package, and Samsung’s I‑CubeE is its own “bridge + RDL” variant. This taxonomy explains why the chart shows NVIDIA shifting to CoWoS‑L at 192 GB HBM3E, AMD persisting on CoWoS‑S at 256‑288 GB, Google/Microsoft staying with CoWoS‑S for v6e/Maia 100, and Amazon opting for CoWoS‑R for Trainium2. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TrendForce, Intel, Samsung Semiconductor Global)

Concrete, high‑confidence facts the committee can anchor on: TSMC explicitly specifies CoWoS‑S to 3.3× reticle with eDTC, CoWoS‑R with 2/2 µm RDL and reliability benefits, and CoWoS‑L with embedded LSI and eDTC; it also states CoWoS‑L volume begins in 2024. NVIDIA confirms H200 at 141 GB HBM3E, and industry sources consistently report Blackwell at 192 GB with CoWoS‑L. AMD publicly positions MI325X/MI350 at 256‑288 GB with HBM3E and has Micron as an HBM3E supplier. Intel’s Gaudi 3 whitepaper confirms TSMC N5 and 128 GB HBM2E. Google states v6e doubles HBM capacity and bandwidth over v5e. TSMC’s CoWoS capacity expansion and pricing actions are corroborated by several trackers, and SK hynix/Micron/Samsung dynamics on HBM share and pricing are well covered by independent sources. These are the ground truths for position sizing. (https://t.co/oi9tKsdRLQ, TSMC, NVIDIA, Wccftech, AMD, Micron Technology, Intel CDRD, Google Cloud, TrendForce)

Bottom line for the portfolio: overweight the upstream bottlenecks (TSMC for CoWoS and wafers; SK hynix and Micron for HBM), add a measured basket of ABF substrate suppliers, and hold selective exposure to equipment and materials levered to advanced packaging and HBM. Underwrite NVIDIA, AMD, and the hyperscalers through the lens of packaging and HBM allocations rather than nominal die roadmaps; each has a credible path, but shipment curves will be determined by CoWoS lines, substrate availability, and HBM bins. The next structural catalysts are 5.5×/9× CoWoS‑L, HBM4 with hybrid bonding, and broader adoption of embedded‑bridge packaging across the industry; all 3 favor the capacity owners and the materials/equipment ecosystem that enables them. (TrendForce, https://t.co/xb6hj4oYpp)

$NVDA NVIDIA’s Rubin CPX is a purpose-built GPU class for the prefill/context phase of inference on 1M+ token workloads, introduced alongside a disaggregated serving model that splits context and generation across different processors. The technical blog and press release specify that each Rubin CPX delivers 30 PFLOPS of NVFP4 compute, 128 GB of GDDR7, integrated video encode/decode, and 3x attention acceleration versus GB300 NVL72 baselines. NVIDIA positions CPX as a compute-dense, cost-optimized, monolithic-die part that complements generation-phase Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs inside a rack-scale “Vera Rubin NVL144 CPX” system that integrates 144 CPX GPUs, 144 Rubin GPUs, and 36 Vera CPUs. At the rack level, NVIDIA cites 8 exaFLOPS of NVFP4, 100 TB of high-speed memory, and 1.7 PB/s aggregate memory bandwidth, claiming 7.5x the AI performance of GB300 NVL72. Availability is targeted for end-2026. These are aggressive, rack-level economics intended to monetize long-context inference (coding and video) with a stated ROI claim of 30x–50x, framed as $5B of “token revenue” per $100M CAPEX at scale; while promotional, the direction of travel is clear: NVIDIA wants to convert the rising cost/latency of extreme-context tokens into a systems-level upsell beyond today’s GB200/GB300. (NVIDIA Developer, NVIDIA Newsroom)

The architectural rationale is sound. Context/prefill is token-parallel and compute-bound; generation is autoregressive and memory-bandwidth-bound. Co-locating both phases on the same GPU wastes resources under long inputs: compute saturates during prefill, then memory fabrics dominate during decode. NVIDIA’s disaggregated serving, orchestrated by the open-source Dynamo framework, routes requests, manages KV caches across nodes, and exploits hierarchical caching and data-movement paths to minimize recomputation and TTFT. NVIDIA has already demonstrated material per-GPU throughput gains from disaggregated serving in MLPerf v5.1 on GB200/GB300 for interactive scenarios, indicating that the scheduler, router, and comms layers can translate into real-world throughput per dollar improvements. Rubin CPX is, in effect, a specialized prefill engine dropped into this disaggregated topology to accelerate the dominant cost center for long contexts. The strategic bet is that system-level throughput gains from specialization plus NVFP4 quantization of weights and FP8 KV caches continue to compress cost/token faster than model growth inflates token counts. (NVIDIA Developer, NVIDIA Docs)

Demand drivers center on 2 high-value domains: code and video. For code, agentic systems need to reason over entire repositories, dependency graphs, and historical context spanning many files and sessions—turning coding copilots into software collaborators tied to enterprise development environments. For video, NVIDIA highlights that 1 hour of content can map to roughly 1M tokens and requires tight coupling of long-context attention with video codecs; CPX integrates video encode/decode with long-context acceleration to collapse that pipeline into a single chip for the context stage. NVIDIA named early lighthouse customers and partners in coding and video to underscore near-term applicability. While not every workload needs 1M tokens, the share of prefill-heavy jobs is rising due to multi-step reasoning, RAG over larger corpora, and tool-using agents with persistent memory; that supports a dedicated context accelerator if and only if the serving stack can keep KV caches hot and route queries to minimize recomputation. (NVIDIA Newsroom, Network World)

The most important economic change is the use of a monolithic die with GDDR7 rather than HBM for CPX. HBM scarcity and packaging constraints have been key supply-side throttles. A GDDR7-based, monolithic context accelerator can be cheaper to build at scale, easier to source, and less dependent on advanced 2.5D packaging, while still feeding NVFP4 math at high rates for attention/prefill. Because prefill is compute-dense and less sensitive to HBM-like bandwidth than generation-heavy decode, the GDDR7 trade-off is attractive in a disaggregated pipeline. If the 3x attention acceleration versus GB300 NVL72 holds in production and Dynamo consistently routes to hot caches, CPX should reduce cost per input token and TTFT for long contexts while increasing overall cluster utilization. The heavy bundling—Rubin CPX + Rubin GPUs + Vera CPUs + Quantum‑X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum‑XGS Ethernet + ConnectX‑9 SuperNICs + AI Enterprise/NIM microservices—simultaneously expands NVIDIA’s per-rack ASP and deepens software lock-in. The flip side is that the ROI math depends on sustained high utilization of prefill engines and on the frequency with which workloads truly need 0.5M–1M+ tokens versus algorithmic techniques that prune, compress, or stream context more efficiently. (NVIDIA Newsroom, NVIDIA Developer)

From a competitive perspective, AMD’s 2024–2026 roadmap has focused on large HBM footprints per accelerator to keep more of the model and KV cache resident, e.g., MI325X with 256 GB HBM3e and 6 TB/s bandwidth, and next-gen MI350X with expanded low-precision data types and up to 288 GB HBM3e and 8 TB/s bandwidth. That approach is well-suited to decode-heavy and medium-context jobs and competes on cost/TCO where software stacks are mature (vLLM/ROCm) and for customers prioritizing memory capacity per device. NVIDIA’s counter with CPX is not “more HBM,” but a system-level division of labor that potentially scales better at 1M-token prefill. Google’s TPU v5e and similar price-optimized inference platforms emphasize cost/token via software and fabric optimization rather than a context-specialized chip. The main question through 2026 is whether hyperscalers lean into disaggregation plus specialization (NVIDIA’s thesis) or continue to extract cost efficiencies via large HBM devices and networking/fleet-level caches without adding a new processor class (AMD/TPU trajectory). Timelines matter: Rubin CPX availability is end-2026, leaving a multi-quarter window in which GB300 NVL72, AMD MI325X/MI350X, and TPUs set customer habits and software defaults. (AMD, Google Cloud, NVIDIA Newsroom)

Investment implications for NVIDIA are significant. First, CPX increases the TAM and the “rack bill of materials” NVIDIA can capture per deployment by adding a new silicon type that is tightly integrated into an already sticky software stack (Dynamo, TensorRT‑LLM, NIM, AI Enterprise). Second, substituting GDDR7 for HBM on a large fraction of prefill compute shifts supply constraints away from HBM packaging and should improve shipment elasticity, smoothing revenue recognition and reducing lead-time risk for inference-heavy builds. Third, CPX’s alignment with long-context workloads in coding and video is strategically astute: these are enterprise monetization vectors with measurable productivity and content-generation outputs, supporting premium token pricing and higher willingness to pay for TTFT reductions and latency guarantees. Fourth, by tying CPX to Quantum‑X800/Spectrum‑XGS and ConnectX‑9, NVIDIA preserves and expands its networking attach. The primary near-term caveat is timing: with availability at end-2026, CPX is unlikely to impact FY26 materially; it is more of a FY27 revenue driver unless NVIDIA books early MGX platform commits. Given NVIDIA’s claim that a fully built NVL144 CPX rack can enable $5B revenue per $100M CAPEX, even partial realization of this thesis can create a second-wave inference CAPEX cycle focused on long-context and agentic systems. We would treat NVIDIA’s ROI multiple as directional rather than literal, but the mechanism—higher utilization and lower cost/token for large contexts—has strong first-principles support. (NVIDIA Newsroom)

For AMD, CPX raises the performance bar specifically on long-context prefill. MI325X/MI350X will remain competitive on decode-heavy or medium-context inference and on generalized training/inference TCO, especially where ROCm stacks are mature and customers value memory-per-accelerator over a new processor category. However, if disaggregation plus CPX becomes the default design pattern for agents, coding copilots, and generative video, AMD may need to lean harder into software-level KV cache routing, memory pooling, and fabric optimizations to avoid ceding long-context economics to NVIDIA’s full-stack solution. AMD’s near-term advantage is availability: MI325X is shipping, MI350X is slated for 2025, so AMD can accrue share and relationships before CPX lands. The competitive watch item is whether customers report stable, high utilization under disaggregated serving and quantized KV caches on NVIDIA stacks; if they do, system-level TCO could tilt toward NVIDIA again in 2026–2027. (AMD)

For the broader supply chain, CPX implies stronger demand for NVIDIA networking (InfiniBand and Spectrum‑XGS Ethernet) and for GDDR7 suppliers, somewhat de-risking the HBM bottleneck while still keeping HBM demand elevated for generation-phase Rubin GPUs. ODMs/OEMs with MGX capability and high-density rack integration stand to benefit. Competitors in KV cache externalization and memory pooling may see mixed effects: if Dynamo’s cache routing keeps hit rates high within the NVIDIA fabric, demand for external memory pools could be curbed; alternatively, for extreme contexts beyond 1M tokens, external DDR5 pools over 400G/800G Ethernet could remain complementary. The state of the art is moving quickly, and NVIDIA’s ability to bundle software and silicon gives it an edge in converting these plumbing choices into revenue. (Amazon Web Services, Inc.)

Key risks and what to watch. 1) Software maturity and reproducibility: the MLPerf wins and blog demos need to translate to multi-tenant, production workloads with real SLAs, tail-latency controls, and dynamic load shaping. Evidence to monitor includes third-party MLPerf submissions and customer case studies showing per-rack TTFT, ITL, and cost/token under 1M-token inputs. 2) Utilization risk: the ROI math is ultrasensitive to context-heavy utilization. If algorithmic techniques—KV cache reuse, chunked prefill, retrieval compression, streaming attention, speculative decoding, and caching across sessions—meaningfully reduce context compute, the specialized CPX layer could be underutilized. 3) Availability and supply risk: end-2026 delivery leaves room for slippage; competitor platforms shipping in 2025–2026 can entrench tooling and developer mindshare. 4) Power and cooling: while CPX’s monolithic GDDR7 design likely has a simpler thermal profile than multi-stack HBM devices, overall rack power with 144 CPX + 144 Rubin + 36 Vera will be material; we need concrete power envelopes and site-level PUE assumptions before underwriting ROI at scale. 5) Pricing and bundling: how NVIDIA prices CPX relative to GB300-class systems will determine whether customers see CPX as accretive or duplicative CAPEX.

Actionable positioning. Overweight NVIDIA on the thesis that CPX extends the company’s systems moat into long-context inference with a new silicon beachhead that is supply-friendlier than HBM-intensive designs, while reinforcing networking and software attach. Treat CPX as a 2026–2027 monetization driver layered atop ongoing Blackwell Ultra/NVL72 ramps in 2025–2026, not as a near-term catalyst. Accrue exposure to NVIDIA networking and select GDDR7 suppliers as second-order beneficiaries. Maintain constructive but selective exposure to AMD on availability and memory-capacity leadership through 2025–2026, but watch for customer traction specifically on long-context jobs; if NVIDIA’s disaggregation pattern becomes standard, consider a relative value tilt back toward NVIDIA-linked ecosystem names. For hyperscaler CAPEX, the read-through is a second wave of inference spend specifically for agents/coding/video; we expect buyers to pilot disaggregated pipelines in 2025 and begin CPX-inclusive rollouts in late 2026 where utilization models are convincing. (NVIDIA Developer, NVIDIA Newsroom)

Bottom line, Rubin CPX is not just another accelerator; it is a system-level argument that the economics of 1M-token context are best solved by specialization and orchestration. If the claimed 3x attention acceleration, 7.5x rack-level uplift, and the software stack’s cache-aware routing hold in customer deployments, the prefill bottleneck becomes a monetizable product tier that expands NVIDIA’s per-rack revenue and strengthens full-stack differentiation. If, conversely, algorithmic and software advances shrink effective context or cache misses remain high in practice, CPX uptake could be slower and more concentrated in video and top-end coding agents. The burden of proof now shifts to early lighthouse users and third-party benchmarks to validate utilization, latency, and cost/token claims at scale. (NVIDIA Developer, NVIDIA Newsroom)
