Flash/NAND is now a first‑class resource in generative AI infrastructure rather than a passive repository. In the training path, datasets flow from object stores or shared filesystems into local NVMe tiers on the GPU hosts, then over GPUDirect Storage DMA paths straight into HBM; in the reverse direction, large periodic checkpoints are flushed back to flash before being drained to capacity tiers. NVIDIA’s own DGX storage reference architecture codifies this, calling for single‑node read bandwidth between 4–40 GB/s and write bandwidth between 2–20 GB/s depending on model type, and explicitly noting that checkpoint files can be “terabytes in size” and are synchronous blockers—hence the need for high‑throughput, low‑latency NVMe on each accelerator node. The same guidance recommends treating local NVMe as a cache or staging tier to avoid saturating the networked store, and pairs that with GPUDirect Storage so data moves directly between NVMe and GPU memory with minimal CPU overhead. This is the architectural reason flash rides alongside every modern AI GPU and why flash bandwidth and capacity scale with the number of accelerators deployed.  ￼

On NVIDIA’s rack‑scale platforms, the flash footprint is explicit and material. A GB200 NVL72 rack contains 18 compute trays; each tray integrates 2 Grace CPUs and 4 Blackwell GPUs and, crucially, 8 hot‑plug E1.S SSDs plus an M.2 boot device. HPE’s QuickSpecs list the baseline as 8×3.84 TB E1.S per tray, yielding 30.72 TB of node‑local NVMe. At full rack scale that is 18×30.72 TB = 552.96 TB of local flash before counting any disaggregated NVMe shelves in the same aisle. The same document shows 18 M.2 OS devices at 1.98 TB each, a non‑trivial but secondary contributor. In cloud form factors, Microsoft’s ND GB200 v6 advertises 4 local NVMe disks totaling 16 TB per host for the same purpose—fast data staging, scratch, and spill. On prior‑gen DGX H100 nodes, NVIDIA shipped 8×3.84 TB U.2 plus dual 1.92 TB M.2 OS devices, a configuration that has become a de facto minimum for 8‑GPU training boxes and a useful proxy for non‑NVLink systems. These platform‑level facts anchor flash content per GPU at roughly 7–16 TB depending on the node design and drive capacities selected.  ￼

AMD‑based AI servers follow the same storage physics. The Instinct MI350X carries 288 GB of HBM3E at 8 TB/s per GPU, so IO starvation is a real risk without robust NVMe tiers. Reference MI350X systems from OEMs show 8–12 front‑accessible U.2/U.3 bays per 8‑GPU chassis, with additional M.2 slots for OS or metadata. Configured with 15.36 TB TLC or QLC, that puts 122–184 TB of node‑local flash under a single 8‑GPU roof, most of which is used for local caching, preprocessed shard staging, and checkpoint buffering. Fundamentally, MI350X compute density raises the same storage requirement curve as GB200: per‑GPU flash capacity and bandwidth need to scale to keep accelerators fed and to ensure training resiliency.  ￼

Disaggregation adds a second engine of flash demand in AI “factories.” To keep accelerators busy across many nodes, hyperscalers deploy NVMe‑oF JBOFs and Ethernet‑attached “bunches of flash,” frequently fronted by DPUs. A typical JBOF with 24 U.2 or 36 E3.S bays turns into 1.5–2.2 PB of flash when populated with today’s 61.44 TB QLC drives, and can deliver 100+ GB/s per shelf with the right fabric and controller. Supermicro’s BlueField‑powered JBOF shows how the DPU terminates NVMe‑oF and acts as a PCIe root for the SSDs to minimize host CPU involvement, while GPUDirect Storage lets these shelves DMA straight into GPU memory at tens of GB/s per node. Meta’s RSC is the canonical at‑scale example: its storage system was architected for 16 TB/s and exabyte‑class capacity, with local and networked flash caches absorbing “first epoch” reads and accelerating non‑sequential access. As model sizes and dataset heterogeneity climb, this pooled NVMe layer grows faster than host‑local flash because it amortizes bandwidth across many accelerators and shortens time‑to‑first‑epoch.  ￼

Inference is becoming an equally important flash consumer. Two emerging patterns drive this: first, model weight staging for rapid cold starts and model swaps, especially with multi‑model serving, and second, tiered KV‑cache architectures that spill less‑recent attention keys/values to NVMe rather than DRAM or GPU memory. Open‑source stacks and vendors now describe disk‑resident KV caches that sharply raise hit rates on multi‑turn conversations; at cluster scale, systems like VAST’s VUA create global NVMe‑backed prefix caches that shrink time‑to‑first‑token, effectively “stretching” GPU memory with flash. The economic lever is straightforward: NVMe is far cheaper per GB than HBM or DDR5, so every percentage point of cache spilled to flash diverts budget to GPUs while raising utilization. That dynamic pushes significant flash attach into inference pods that may be far more numerous than training racks.  ￼

Drive technology is simultaneously removing capacity constraints and altering mix. Shipping enterprise NVMe spans from 7.68 TB TLC to 61.44 TB and 122.88 TB QLC today, with announced 122 TB E3.S and 245 TB E3.L on Micron’s 6600 ION roadmap and 122.88 TB already shown by Solidigm’s D5‑P5336. The shift to EDSFF E1.S/E3.S raises per‑node slots, power envelopes, and serviceability, which—combined with rising per‑drive capacities—pushes per‑rack flash into multi‑petabyte territory without explosive slot counts. Net effect: bit growth per AI rack accelerates even if the number of drives per node stays flat; with 18 compute trays, a baseline GB200 NVL72 already embeds ~0.55 PB of local flash using 3.84 TB E1.S, and the same chassis can scale its cache by simply slotting higher‑capacity media or adding a small number of JBOFs. This is a structurally different demand curve than classic CPU server refresh cycles.  ￼

Translating architecture into NAND bit demand: the scalar is “flash per accelerator.” With GB200 NVL72, the baseline works out to ~7.68 TB of NVMe per GPU from local E1.S alone; MI350X 8‑GPU boxes configured with 8×15.36 TB sit around 15.36 TB per GPU. Even assuming conservative adoption—say, 4–8 TB/GPU local plus 0.5–1.5 PB of pooled JBOF flash per rack—the math compounds fast. At 1,000 racks, that is roughly 0.5 EB of local NVMe plus 0.5–1.5 EB of pooled flash; at 10,000 racks, it is 5–20 EB, and that excludes downstream all‑flash arrays feeding pre‑processing, RAG indices, and vector databases attached to inference farms. Because these racks tend to be storage‑balanced at deployment and then upgraded in place as datasets and model catalogs grow, flash procurement is not a 1‑and‑done event; it repeats as more capacity is carved out for caching, new models, and higher QLC layer densities. The flow‑through to enterprise SSD revenue is already visible in quarterly data as Blackwell and other AI platforms ramp.  ￼

Pricing and supply are tightening around the enterprise SSD segment as AI growth collides with a still‑oligopolistic NAND industry. TrendForce has flagged enterprise SSD revenue up 12.7% QoQ in 2Q25 on AI server builds, and has also pointed to 3Q25 NAND contract price increases of 5–10% on low finished‑goods inventories; recent commentary additionally highlights periodic shortages in controller IC substrates and even DRAMs used as drive cache, which can pinch availability at the high‑capacity end. While the cyclical NAND industry can add die‑level supply with each node, high‑cap QLC drives depend on controller readiness, PCIe Gen5/Gen6 platform support, and the EDSFF supply chain, so enterprise SSD supply can be temporarily inelastic—exactly when hyperscalers want to lock in multi‑quarter volumes. The medium‑term counterweight is die density: Micron’s 122 TB E3.S and 245 TB E3.L designs and Solidigm’s 122.88 TB family suggest bit/drive will outpace rack slot growth from 2025–2027, which should gradually loosen capacity constraints even if attach per GPU keeps rising.  ￼

Workload mix determines TLC vs QLC demand. Training checkpoints and mixed read/write caches still lean TLC for endurance and QoS predictability, whereas dataset shards, prefix caches, and inference KV caches are mostly read‑dominant and increasingly land on QLC to minimize $/TB. Hyperscalers like Meta have publicly endorsed QLC as a strategic lever for data center economics, and vendors are pushing QLC‑first arrays and 60–122 TB NVMe for AI capacity tiers. That implies a sustained mix shift toward QLC at the rack and array level, with TLC concentrated in the per‑node write‑intensive tiers—exactly where the “hot path” performance and durability matter. Over time, controller‑level wear management and host‑managed placement are expanding QLC’s envelope even for lighter‑write checkpoint and pre‑processing tasks, increasing the proportion of AI‑driven NAND bits that are QLC.  ￼

The near‑term demand impulse is strongest at 2 layers of the stack: node‑local NVMe caches that scale roughly linearly with the accelerator base, and disaggregated NVMe pools that scale with cluster size and model catalog breadth. Inference multiplies the effect because there are more inference nodes than training nodes, and they increasingly rely on NVMe for low‑cost weight staging and KV‑cache tiers. With Blackwell and MI350X ramps, that is enough to swing the enterprise SSD market into periodic undersupply even if total NAND output across mobile and client remains ample. The macro wild cards are hyperscaler capex cadence and platform transitions; a broad slowdown in 2026 capex would temper growth, but the structural attach of flash to GPUs means the floor is higher than in prior cycles. On balance, the generative AI buildout should keep enterprise SSD demand growing faster than aggregate NAND supply through 2026, with pricing power accruing to high‑capacity QLC and to TLC SKUs aimed at write‑heavy training tiers, until 122–245 TB drives are pervasive and controller/EDSFF bottlenecks clear.

post.text:
$SNDK $MU High-bandwidth memory (HBM) remains the performance and bandwidth anchor for AI server GPUs, but the industry is probing whether a flash-based, on‑package complement can relieve HBM’s persistent capacity, cost, and supply constraints. SanDisk’s “High‑Bandwidth Flash” (HBF) is the most concrete proposal to date: a NAND‑based, TSV‑stacked device intended to sit on the GPU interposer like an HBM stack, trading orders‑of‑magnitude higher access latency for vastly higher capacity and non‑volatility while claiming to sustain comparable read bandwidth for inference. SanDisk asserts that HBF can offer 8–16× HBM capacity at similar price points and read bandwidth, with simulations showing HBF within 2.2% of a hypothetical unlimited‑capacity HBM system on Llama 3.1 405B; the company targets first HBF samples in 2H26 and early 2027 sampling of inference devices. SanDisk has also announced an MoU with SK hynix to work toward a standard and ecosystem. These are vendor claims rather than independent benchmarks, but they outline a credible memory‑centric roadmap that could reshape inference system design if realized.  ￼

HBM’s technical and market position is clear. It is 3D‑stacked DRAM with a 1024‑bit (HBM3/3E) to 2048‑bit (HBM4) bus per stack, delivering per‑stack bandwidths around 1.0–1.2 TB/s for HBM3E at 8–9.6 Gbps/pin, and moving to wider, faster links and custom base dies with HBM4. Contemporary accelerators such as NVIDIA B100/B200 expose up to roughly 8 TB/s aggregate HBM bandwidth with 192 GB HBM3E, and NVLink 5 at 1.8 TB/s per GPU for scale‑out. HBM is expensive and packaging‑intensive, but it supplies the deterministic bandwidth and sub‑µs access regime that dense training and high‑QPS inference demand today. Roadmaps into 2026–2027 push capacity and bandwidth further with HBM4, while advanced packaging (e.g., TSMC CoWoS‑L) remains a gating resource.  ￼

SanDisk’s HBF diverges architecturally. It is a NAND stack with a logic/PHY die (via CBA, “CMOS directly Bonded to Array”) bonded to 3D NAND planes and TSV‑connected core dies, sized to be “HBM‑footprint compatible” so it can be co‑packaged on an interposer near the GPU. The Gen1 fact sheet specifies read bandwidth of 1.6 TB/s per stack and 512 GB capacity per 16‑die stack (256 Gb per die), with Gen2 and Gen3 road‑mapped to >2.0 and >3.2 TB/s and up to 1.0–1.5 TB per stack, alongside projected power reductions versus Gen1. As non‑volatile media, HBF eliminates DRAM refresh power and can preserve models across power cycles. SanDisk positions Gen1 explicitly for inference, not training. The packaging images and third‑party coverage indicate HBF would be wired like HBM on the interposer, not attached via PCIe, which is required to reach multi‑TB/s device‑local bandwidths. The vendor also highlights KAIST’s proposed topology with ~100 GB HBM acting as a cache in front of ~1 TB HBF. All of this is plausible given recent NAND I/O advances (Toggle DDR 6.0, CBA), but it remains pre‑silicon and unproven at system level.  ￼

The central trade is latency. HBM random access is typically on the order of 100–150 ns, while even highly‑optimized SLC‑style flash such as Kioxia XL‑Flash or Samsung Z‑NAND achieves single‑digit to tens of µs reads; mainstream TLC/QLC read latency sits in the 40–100 µs class. HBF asserts that bandwidth and smart scheduling can mask this gap for inference weights, and SanDisk’s simulation suggests the penalty can be largely hidden for a 405B‑parameter LLM with an HBM cache. The inference literature supports the direction: “LLM in a Flash” and follow‑ons show that reading larger contiguous chunks, windowing, and tier‑aware scheduling can maintain throughput with weights resident on flash and cached in DRAM/HBM. However, the µs‑scale access times materially constrain workloads: HBF is a read‑mostly tier for model parameters and possibly cold KV data; it is unsuitable for write‑heavy training loops (optimizer states, gradient updates) or hot KV caches that demand nanosecond‑class reuse. In practice, any HBF design for servers must present an on‑package multi‑TB/s read path plus a compiler/runtime that aggressively prefetches and batches weight blocks into HBM.  ￼

HBM’s near‑term outlook remains one of growth and scarcity. HBM3E and HBM4 are ramping, HBM is taking a rising share of DRAM value, and packaging capacity has been the bottleneck for AI GPU shipments. TSMC’s CoWoS output is expanding materially into 2025–2026, but remains tightly allocated; NVIDIA has indicated a migration toward CoWoS‑L with Blackwell, not a reduction in advanced packaging needs. If HBF is realized as an HBM‑site‑compatible stack on the same interposers, it will compete for the same scarce beachfront and could be constrained by the same CoWoS capacity—unless HBF can be built with alternative packaging providers at scale. That implies HBF cannot relieve the packaging bottleneck in 2026–2027; at best it shifts content mix and increases memory bytes per interposer.  ￼

System‑level alternatives are also progressing. Outside the package, GPU‑direct storage and CXL/RDMA memory pooling are maturing quickly and are already deployable. GPUDirect Storage designs can sustain tens of GB/s per GPU from NVMe or NVMe‑oF, with emerging roadmaps from Kioxia and Samsung reviving ultra‑low‑latency flash that aims at 10–100M IOPS SSDs and GPU‑peer‑to‑peer access. Startups like Enfabrica are demonstrating Ethernet‑attached CXL memory appliances that present tens of TB of DDR5 across the rack with RDMA, explicitly targeting KV caches and long‑context inference. These approaches do not deliver on‑package TB/s, but they are real, shipping sooner, and can be scaled independently of CoWoS. As such, HBF will compete not just with HBM but with network‑fabric memory tiers that are improving.  ￼

Economically, HBM carries a structurally higher $/GB than DDR5 due to stacking yields, TSV cost, and advanced packaging; industry tracking consistently frames HBM as several‑times the cost of DDR5, with 2025 HBM pricing still forecast to rise 5–10% amid strong demand. By contrast, high‑capacity enterprise SSDs have reached <$0.10/GB at retail in some cases. If HBF can truly deliver “HBM‑class” read bandwidth at “similar price points” to HBM while providing 8–16× capacity per site, the system BOM equation for inference shifts sharply toward more parameters per GPU and lower model sharding. The caveat is that HBF’s price/performance remains a roadmap claim and the packaging bill of materials will matter; HBF that consumes an HBM site but costs close to an HBM stack still must justify the performance win after latency hiding, controller die area, and software complexity.  ￼

Workload mapping is therefore clear. For training, HBM remains non‑negotiable and is likely to absorb any packaging area available, as write bandwidth, latency, determinism, and symmetry dominate. For high‑QPS inference on dense models at modest context, HBM capacity and bandwidth also dominate, with larger HBM footprints enabling larger batch sizes and better utilization. Where HBF could be most disruptive is very large parameter counts (≥400B), long‑context inference where KV dominates memory footprint, and mixture‑of‑experts with low active parameter sets. In these cases, a design with 100–192 GB of HBM as a read/write cache plus 512 GB–1.5 TB per HBF site as a read‑mostly tier could reduce cross‑GPU sharding, lower interconnect traffic, and increase single‑GPU model residency. The decide‑point is how well vendors can prefetch and pack weight rows to amortize µs‑latency, and whether the KV path—often 40–70% of memory at long context—can be kept in HBM or offloaded to CXL/DDR without stalling decoders. NVIDIA’s own guidance shows KV footprints exploding with context length, which underscores why disaggregated KV tiers are in parallel development.  ￼

Adoption risk is material. HBF requires GPU vendor buy‑in to expose a new on‑package memory type, controller logic on the GPU or in an adjacent base die, and compiler/runtime changes to drive tier‑aware prefetch and eviction with very high concurrency. It also requires a multi‑supplier ecosystem to satisfy hyperscaler qualification. The SK hynix MoU is a positive signal given hynix’s HBM leadership and interposer know‑how, but there is no public commitment from NVIDIA or AMD to ship an HBF‑equipped GPU. Timeline risk is non‑trivial as HBM4 designs are already tracking for 2026 and will be deeply optimized in the software stack by the time HBF samples. The most credible early entry points are inference‑only accelerators or edge devices that prioritize capacity per watt over raw latency, with servers following only if ecosystem and packaging hurdles are cleared.  ￼

Investment implications over 12–36 months are nuanced and asymmetric across the stack. For DRAM vendors, HBM demand remains the central earnings driver through at least 2027 as training and mainstream inference absorb HBM3E/HBM4 capacity; HBF, if successful, is more likely to displace some HBM sites in inference‑focused SKUs than to dent training‑centric GPUs, limiting cannibalization. SK hynix screens best because it leads in HBM today and is positioned as an HBF co‑standard setter, creating an “optionality kicker” without sacrificing HBM share. Samsung also benefits on any HBM4 mix shift and could pair Z‑NAND‑class technology with HBF‑like packaging if the standard opens, preserving strategic flexibility. Micron benefits from HBM TAM acceleration and has less near‑term optionality in on‑package flash, but HBF’s emergence does not impair its HBM growth and could even expand the memory TAM per accelerator if adopted. For NAND vendors, Western Digital/SanDisk and JV‑partner Kioxia have a clear call option: if HBF is standardized and adopted in volume from 2027, the NAND TAM extends into the AI accelerator BOM at premium ASPs, lifting mix, margin, and capital intensity under a more stable demand profile than cyclic client SSDs. In a bull case where 1–2 HBF sites per GPU become standard on inference SKUs, NAND dollars per rack rise and WDC/Kioxia’s relative operating leverage could be meaningful. The bear case is that GPUDirect Storage plus CXL DDR pooling solves enough of the inference memory problem without CoWoS consumption, leaving HBF as niche or edge‑only.  ￼

For foundries and OSATs, HBF is a net positive if it lands, because it increases die count and advanced packaging content per package. But it does not relax CoWoS scarcity; in fact, an HBF+HBM configuration would increase shoreline and interposer routing pressure. TSMC therefore remains a core beneficiary in any memory‑centric scenario, with incremental risk that customers push for organic interposer or alternative 2.5D stacks to diversify capacity. Networking silicon vendors and memory‑fabric startups gain if HBF slips: CXL switch and DPU/NIC providers capture spend for pooled memory and GPUDirect topologies, and this path is already shipping, likely pulling revenue 12–24 months ahead of any HBF ramp.  ￼

Positioning for a TMT portfolio, the base case remains to overweight HBM‑exposed suppliers through the HBM4 transition and maintain exposure to advanced packaging. SK hynix and TSMC are the highest‑conviction beneficiaries on fundamentals and scarcity dynamics. Layer in a measured call option on Western Digital (and by association Kioxia, to the extent your vehicle can express it) as the pure‑play on HBF optionality plus CBA NAND performance leadership. Maintain selective exposure to network memory plays that benefit if HBF is delayed or underperforms, as these are not mutually exclusive with a memory‑centric trend. On the GPU side, HBF adoption would likely appear first as an inference‑only SKU or as a split‑site design that replaces 1–2 HBM stacks with HBF; the clear near‑term read‑through is that NVIDIA and AMD will continue to prioritize HBM bandwidth for mainstream parts and lean on NVLink, GDS, and CXL for capacity. That mix argues against underwriting any near‑term collapse in HBM ASPs or margins; HBF, if anything, extends the memory TAM rather than compresses it, and its latency profile keeps it complementary, not substitutive, for training.  ￼

Key catalysts to watch are hard, falsifiable milestones rather than narratives. The first is a public HBF PHY/controller spec and reference stack from the SanDisk/SK hynix group, including cache‑management semantics, access granularity, and coherency with HBM. The second is a GPU vendor announcement of an HBF‑capable package layout and compiler/runtime support, ideally with microbenchmarks showing sustained per‑stack read >1 TB/s and end‑to‑end inference throughput within a single‑digit percentage of an HBM‑only baseline at large parameter counts. The third is packaging capacity allocation, since HBF cannot scale without guaranteed interposer windows. Absent these, assume HBM retains its choke‑point status and allocate accordingly; if they arrive on SanDisk’s timetable, HBF becomes a real underwriting theme for 2027 inference capex, with upside for WDC/Kioxia and modest mix recalibration for HBM vendors rather than a structural threat.

post.text:
$NVDA $MU $SNDK $RMBS Offloading KV cache and related state from GPU HBM to external tiers rewires the AI inference memory stack and shifts spend from on‑package bandwidth memory toward pooled capacity DRAM. Training remains HBM‑bandwidth‑bound and continues to drive higher HBM per accelerator, but inference increasingly treats HBM as a hot cache for the last N tokens and heavy‑hitter slices, with warm state living in pooled DDR5 accessed over high‑speed transports. That change reduces stranded HBM capacity, raises GPU utilization, and increases total DRAM attached per rack. The practical result for U.S. names with memory exposure is more DDR5 bits shipped into CXL/Ethernet memory appliances and memory‑dense servers, faster adoption of CXL controllers, buffers and retimers, and only a limited displacement of flash in the very specific niche of KV‑cache tiers. NVMe and HDD remain critical for weights, checkpoints, datasets and RAG corpora, but KV cache itself gravitates to pooled DRAM because microsecond latency beats millisecond flash. A simple sizing anchor: if 100,000 inference GPUs are deployed in 8‑GPU servers and each server attaches an average 1.5 TB of pooled DDR5, that is roughly 18 PB of incremental DDR5, or about 150,000 128‑GB RDIMMs, before considering replication or growth in context length and concurrency. That is additive to DDR5 already inside CPU sockets and does not cannibalize HBM used for training.

Micron (MU) is a direct beneficiary. It ships both HBM and DDR5. KV‑offload reduces the need to overprovision HBM for inference headroom but increases total inference capacity served, which tends to expand accelerator fleets rather than shrink them. Training roadmaps keep pushing HBM capacity and bandwidth per device higher, so HBM bit demand continues to compound, while pooled DDR5 becomes a second leg of growth as inference standardizes on multi‑terabyte warm tiers per rack. The mix benefit is meaningful: DDR5 has lower cost per bit than HBM, so units can scale faster; Micron’s leverage to RDIMM density increases as operators move from 64‑GB to 128‑GB and 256‑GB modules to hit multi‑terabyte pools. Near‑term gross‑margin puts and takes come from DDR5 price cycles, but the structural effect is higher DDR5 content per deployed GPU and sustained HBM tightness from training, which is a constructive setup for revenue and utilization through 2026.

Rambus (RMBS) benefits at two layers: interface IP and CXL/DDR5 control. KV‑offload and memory pooling pull more designs onto CXL‑attached memory expanders and require faster DDR5 memory controller PHYs, RCDs/buffers, and security IP for memory appliances. Every pooled‑memory box or CXL DIMM proliferates the attach points for Rambus IP and controller technology. As pooled DDR5 becomes standard in inference racks, license and royalty revenue scale with the number of memory‑attached devices even if the absolute number of GPUs grows at a different pace. The risk is timing: if software stacks under‑deliver on tail‑latency control, customers may defer aggressive offload, but that shifts demand rather than erasing it.

Astera Labs (ALAB) is one of the clearest winners because CXL retimers and memory‑controller SoCs sit directly in the data path of pooled DDR5. KV‑offload raises the value of low‑jitter CXL paths, deterministic latency, and memory expansion modules. As operators move from single‑node memory expansion to rack‑level pooling, the number of CXL endpoints and retimers per rack rises, which drives unit and content growth for Astera’s Aries/Leo‑class products. The key variable is how quickly hyperscalers jump from pilot to broad rollout; the strategic direction is favorable and offload economics accelerate that adoption.

Western Digital (WDC) has a mixed read‑through. Flash‑based KV tiers lose share to pooled DDR5 for strict latency workloads because DRAM’s microsecond access beats NVMe’s millisecond behavior even with aggressive prefetch. That trims a prospective, still‑nascent niche for SSDs in the KV role. Offsetting that, AI growth continues to expand demand for high‑performance NVMe for prefill, checkpoints and feature stores, and for high‑capacity HDD for foundation model training sets, logs and RAG corpora. Net, KV‑offload is a modest headwind to the specific “flash‑as‑KV” narrative but does not impair the larger AI storage tailwinds; WDC’s outcome depends more on NAND pricing discipline and enterprise SSD share than on KV‑offload per se. If “SNDK” on your list is the legacy SanDisk line item, the economic exposure is already consolidated inside WDC.

Seagate (STX) is largely neutral to KV‑offload. HDDs are not competitive for KV due to latency, but they remain the cost‑per‑bit backbone for cold and warm AI data. As inference scales, the surrounding data lake, telemetry and retrieval indices grow, which supports nearline capacity HDD shipments. The company’s AI narrative hinges on exabyte demand and helium platform mix, not on KV‑offload mechanics; the latter has little direct impact.

Pure Storage (PSTG) faces a nuanced setup. In the narrow KV‑cache role, pooled DDR5 is the superior technical fit, so arrays positioned as KV backends will see limited uptake. In the broader AI pipeline, Pure’s all‑flash systems remain relevant for high‑IOPS prefill, checkpoints, fast training datasets, vector stores and model artifact storage where predictable latency and data‑reduction matter. As more operators lean into pooled DRAM for KV, Pure’s product and go‑to‑market need to emphasize AI data services rather than KV offload specifically. The company can still win significant AI spend, but the KV‑cache sub‑narrative is likely to consolidate around DRAM pools, not flash arrays, which slightly lowers upside optionality versus the most bullish AI‑storage takes.

NetApp (NTAP) is similar to Pure on direction but with a different mix. ONTAP and the company’s data‑management stack remain embedded with enterprises modernizing for AI. KV‑offload tilts the architecture away from using SSD as a KV tier, but NetApp’s opportunity in AI remains in data pipelines, snapshotting, replication, hybrid cloud placement and compliant data governance. The company’s exposure to the KV‑specific change is modest; success will track enterprise AI adoption curves and the ability to certify and reference‑architect with major AI platforms rather than KV economics.

Netlist (NLST) has high‑beta optionality. KV‑offload and memory pooling increase unit demand for high‑capacity RDIMMs and, potentially, for CXL memory modules. That plays to Netlist’s product focus and patent portfolio. The constraints are scale, supply assurance and litigation overhangs. If the market standardizes on pooled DDR5 and Netlist secures either volume programs or favorable licensing outcomes, upside can be significant; if not, the company may remain a niche supplier while larger OEMs capture the bulk of pooled RDIMM growth. This is a classic asymmetric setup with execution and legal risk dominating fundamentals.

Microchip (MCHP) should see steady tailwinds. Pooled memory and high‑port‑count NICs increase the need for PCIe Gen5/Gen6 retimers, switches, timing, clocking and signal‑integrity components—the legacy Microsemi portfolio. As CXL memory expanders and high‑lane‑count SuperNICs proliferate, so does demand for these enabling parts. The company is not a DRAM vendor, but it monetizes the plumbing that makes pooled DRAM viable at rack scale, and KV‑offload amplifies that plumbing attach.

“PENG” on the list is not a standard memory ticker; if this is intended to represent Penguin Solutions under SGH or another U.S. memory‑dense platform vendor, the read‑through would be positive. Memory‑optimized servers and CXL memory appliances are directly aligned with KV‑offload adoption. If it refers to a different company, the correct mapping depends on whether that company sells DRAM modules, CXL hardware, or storage arrays; DRAM and CXL exposure is a tailwind, pure storage exposure is a mixed read as described above.

Bottom‑up portfolio implications are to overweight the DDR5/CXL value chain and the memory‑connectivity enablers, stay constructive but selective on AI‑storage names, and treat HDD as largely orthogonal to KV‑offload. For DDR5 and CXL, the adoption curve is likely 2025 pilots broadening into 2026 standardization, with rising per‑rack DRAM pools as context windows, multimodal tokens and concurrency expand. For flash arrays, the best outcomes come from leaning into AI data services and reference architectures rather than pitching flash as a KV tier. For HBM, do not underweight on the assumption of substitution: training keeps HBM structurally tight, and inference growth tends to increase total accelerator count even as pooled DDR5 reduces wasted HBM headroom. The key risks to this view are slower‑than‑expected software maturity for KV block managers, congestion/tail issues that force operators to pin more state in HBM, and a macro pause in AI capex; the upside risk is faster standardization on pooled DRAM that pushes DDR5 and CXL volumes above current expectations.

post.text:
$SNDK SanDisk has re-emerged as a pure‑play NAND franchise with a cleaner focus, a disciplined supply posture, and a differentiated technology roadmap that is starting to matter to hyperscalers. The separation from Western Digital closed in 2‑2025, and SNDK now trades on Nasdaq with the Kioxia Flash Ventures JV as its manufacturing backbone and co‑R&D engine; the JV lets SanDisk invest and scale like a top‑tier vendor while keeping capital intensity below historical industry averages. Management’s operating stance is explicit: run for profit and cash, not elasticity‑driven share, and keep wafer starts and nodal migrations tightly gated to demand. That is paired with a product strategy anchored on BiCS8 (218‑layer CBA wafer‑bonded NAND) across client and consumer, a two‑track enterprise SSD roadmap (compute‑centric PCIe Gen5/Gen6 TLC and capacity‑centric UltraQLC), and a longer‑dated bet on High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) to open a new memory tier for inference. The result is a portfolio and supply stance aligned to a NAND market that management and several third parties now characterize as structurally tight through at least 2026, with pricing power returning even as cost tailwinds from BiCS8 begin to show through. In our view the investment debate collapses into 3 questions: 1) how durable is the undersupply and pricing uptrend, 2) how quickly and how far can gross margin expand as BiCS8 mix rises and underutilization/start‑up drag fades, and 3) how much of the enterprise SSD “wedge” SanDisk can credibly capture over the next 4‑6 quarters. On 1), multiple reads corroborate a tight market and rising contract prices; on 2), the glidepath looks visible if not linear; on 3), the proof will be in hyperscaler qualifications and repeat orders, where momentum is building but still early.  ￼

The near‑term setup is constructive. June‑quarter revenue was $1.901B with non‑GAAP EPS $0.29; bit shipments and ASPs were both up mid‑single‑digits, inventory days fell from 150 to 135, and management reduced long‑term debt while reiterating a roadmap to net cash. For September‑quarter guide, revenue is $2.10B–$2.20B (+13% q/q at midpoint), gross margin is 28.5%–29.5% but still burdened by $10M–$15M of underutilization and ~$60M of FAB start‑up costs tied to BiCS8. Excluding those charges, implied gross margin is already low‑30s% and management expects a 2‑step reduction in start‑up costs by fiscal Q3 with underutilization approaching zero as supply/demand tightness persists. Free cash flow is guided positive, with net debt continuing to decline. This cadence—pricing lift plus lower cost drag—underpins a path to through‑cycle 35% gross margin in the next 2–3 quarters if market tightness holds and BiCS8 mix ramps as planned.

Supply/demand and pricing are the crux. SanDisk increased prices in the channel cohort by ~10% in September, and the company expects broader pricing to lift as quarterly negotiations roll through client OEMs and cloud; management continues to call for undersupply through calendar 2026 as industry CapEx stays constrained and node conversions (which are far more capital intensive in 3D NAND) are paced rather than pushed. Third‑party trackers corroborate a pricing inflection: TrendForce flagged 3Q25 NAND contract prices up 5%–10% with tightness stretching into 2026, and press coverage in late Q3/Q4 has documented further ASP momentum and selective vendor quoting pauses as inventories tightened. Against that backdrop, Kioxia/SanDisk’s BiCS8 ramp provides cost‑per‑bit relief just as pricing improves—management plans to take BiCS8 from ~7% of bits in F4Q25 to 40%–50% of bits by F4Q26, flipping a year of cost headwinds into a year of tailwinds. This is the right cycle setup for a NAND supplier: rising ASPs while the cost curve inflects down. The open risk is a surprise supply response, most notably from YMTC; recent reports point to a $3B Wuhan Phase III effort and a possible ~50k wpm expansion into 2026, but as of now the aggregate industry stance remains disciplined and U.S. tariff policy has lifted the effective hurdle rate on Chinese chip imports into the U.S. to 50%, which should limit spill‑over in SanDisk’s core markets.   ￼  ￼  ￼  ￼  ￼

The data center wedge is real and expanding, but still a “prove‑it” execution item. In F4Q25, data center represented “over 12%” of shipped bits, up from 13% for the year, with two distinct product tracks. First, a compute‑centric eSSD has been in market for ~1 year, qualified at 1 hyperscaler and now undergoing qualification at a second, and it was the first enterprise SSD certified within NVIDIA’s reference architecture, which should ease inclusion in GB300‑class AI factories. Second, the storage‑centric capacity platform—Stargate—anchors SanDisk’s UltraQLC strategy, with 128TB/256TB Gen5 drives now in customer hands for initial qualifications and a roadmap to 512TB and 1PB thereafter. Management targeted 256TB qualifications at several Tier‑1 customers by FYE26, implying revenue impact skewed to late FY26/FY27. The economic pitch is simple: predictable, cache‑less QLC performance at extreme densities with competitive TCO for “fast data lakes” that sit close to accelerated compute, where write patterns are manageable and read throughput and power efficiency dominate. If the 256TB class becomes a de‑facto capacity point for AI data corpora, SanDisk’s early mover advantage, co‑designed controller, and BiCS8 QLC characteristics will matter. The flip side is that hyperscaler qualification cycles are long and device behavior under mixed workloads will be scrutinized; investors should expect a series of discrete design‑in updates rather than a straight‑line ramp, and eSSD mix will remain sensitive to relative pricing versus nearline HDD.   ￼  ￼

BiCS8 is a meaningful architectural step, not just a layer‑count bump. The CMOS‑Bonded‑Array approach bonds a logic wafer to the cell array wafer, separating command/address buses from data I/O and enabling higher interface speeds and more parallelism at similar footprint. Kioxia has publicly disclosed Toggle DDR6.0 at up to 4.8Gb/s and the JV points to better performance‑per‑watt and QLC behavior at scale; critically, SanDisk is leaning into this with system‑level techniques such as “Direct Write QLC” to avoid pseudo‑SLC caches and Dynamic Frequency Scaling to tune power/performance. For the investment case, the takeaway is not the absolute benchmark but the cost and reliability envelope: BiCS8 should unlock per‑GB cost downs as mix rises in FY26 while sustaining enterprise‑class QLC endurance profiles, and that is what ultimately expands gross margin. The key operational risk is yield/maturity on the new bonded flow at high volume and managing the transition away from the exceptionally mature BiCS5 base.  ￼  ￼

HBF is longer‑dated but strategically important optionality. SanDisk and SK hynix are collaborating to standardize HBF as an industry specification, with die samples guided for 2H26 and controller samples in early 2027. HBF won “Best of Show, Most Innovative Technology” at FMS 2025 and targets a memory‑tier role where high bandwidth is required but DRAM/HBM capacity, cost, and power are limiting. The company’s framing is not “HBM replacement” but “enable inference everywhere”—phones, PCs, and the cloud—by marrying flash’s density and non‑volatility with controller and packaging techniques to deliver higher bandwidth than today’s SSD tier. Commercial impact should be modeled as 2027+ and highly scenario‑dependent; nevertheless, the path to a standard with a top‑2 memory peer plus a technical advisory board reduces execution risk versus a go‑it‑alone approach and keeps SanDisk at the table as the memory hierarchy evolves. For portfolio construction, treat HBF as a free call option embedded in the equity rather than a near‑term driver.  ￼

Client and consumer remain durable cash engines while the data center ramps. BiCS8 client SSDs are now qualified across all major PC OEMs and management is seeing rising average capacity per device in both smartphones and PCs as AI‑capable client platforms roll out. Consumer remains strategically important for brand and distribution leverage; the company has already implemented price increases in channel SKUs and is seeing healthy sell‑through on BiCS5 while introducing higher‑performance USB4 portable SSDs and co‑branded gaming expansions. The mix strategy is straightforward: use the breadth of end‑markets—consumer, client, gaming, enterprise—to maximize price‑times‑bits each quarter as supply stays tight. The risk here is that consumer elasticity can amplify volatility if the channel balks at price moves, but management’s cadence of quarterly price/volume negotiations mitigates this.  ￼

Valuation dispersion reflects the fork in the road on margins and the enterprise SSD wedge. On one end, Barclays stays Equal Weight with a $39 PT, seeing tailwinds but waiting for more evidence that enterprise SSD share can break out and that gross margins can hold mid‑30s% through‑cycle. Wells Fargo is Equal Weight at $50 but explicitly highlights a 2H FY26 setup with underutilization largely gone and start‑up costs materially lower, while Mizuho is Outperform at $57, arguing the NAND cycle is turning with customers on allocation and pricing up into December/March as BiCS8 scales. GF Securities is the outlier with a $132 PT predicated on a stronger eSSD upcycle, NAND bit demand growth >20% in 2026 against ~15% supply growth (including YMTC), and the view that CSP eSSD orders are creating an “HBM moment for NAND.” Across these, Mizuho’s model implies SNDK at ~0.8x FY26 revenue and a modest premium P/E to peers on FY26 EPS, which is reasonable if gross margin breaks sustainably above 30% and eSSD wins accumulate, but aggressive if ASP momentum fades. For positioning, that spread argues for a risk‑managed long biased to execution milestones rather than a “set‑and‑forget” bet on the 2027 narrative.

Macro and buyer power matter. Hyperscaler data‑center CapEx is the ultimate demand backstop for data center flash; Dell’Oro now projects data‑center CapEx to compound at 21% through 2029 with accelerators already ~⅓ of spend, and sell‑side capex tallies for 2025–2026 have been moving higher through the summer, albeit with debates about a 2026 digestion. If 2026 capex moderates from 2025 peaks, the mix could still favor storage near GPUs as inference scales, but the slope of ASP increases would flatten. The more acute policy risk is trade/tariff volatility; the U.S. raised the Section 301 rate on Chinese semiconductors to 50% by 2025, which indirectly supports pricing power among non‑Chinese suppliers but can also distort regional mix and channel timing. YMTC’s expansion path is an additional watch item; if the company can translate capital into qualified, exportable enterprise SSD supply despite restrictions, it would challenge the undersupply thesis.  ￼  ￼  ￼

Investment implications for the portfolio are as follows. First, the cycle call is favorable: undersupply prints, observed price hikes, and a visible cost down tailwind form a classic NAND “sweet spot” for operating leverage in FY26. In that scenario, every 1% sequential ASP lift combined with 2–3 pts of BiCS8 mix accretion disproportionately drops to gross margin as start‑up/underutilization fade; this is why multiple shops expect a march toward mid‑30s% gross margin into late FY26. Second, the enterprise SSD wedge is the swing factor for the multiple. If SanDisk moves from mid‑ to high‑single‑digit eSSD share toward low‑teens share over the next 4–6 quarters, with 256TB qualifications converting to volume and the compute SSD line broadening, the stock warrants a peer‑premium P/E on FY26–FY27 EPS and a rerate on EV/sales toward 1x as the narrative shifts from “consumer brand with JV” to “data center supplier with optionality.” Third, HBF is a 2027+ call option; it should not be in the base case but adds convexity if the inference memory tier coalesces around an HBF‑like construct. Fourth, risks are manageable but non‑trivial: a 2026 capex digestion or a faster‑than‑expected YMTC ramp would compress ASP trajectories; qualification slips on UltraQLC would push revenue right and dent the mix thesis; yield learning on BiCS8 must hold as mix rises; and channel pushback could blunt consumer price actions. Fifth, the balance sheet is trending to net cash and free cash flow is positive even during the BiCS8 start‑up bulge, which supports buyback capacity and cushions execution volatility.

Actionably, for a multi‑manager book with strict risk limits, we would treat SNDK as a cyclical long with idiosyncratic catalysts and manage it as a 2‑leg position. Leg 1 is a core 12‑month long to capture the ASP‑plus‑cost‑down operating leverage and the fade of start‑up/underutilization, sized to withstand 20% drawdowns tied to macro capex headlines. Leg 2 is a catalyst sleeve sized smaller and traded tactically around quarterly hyperscaler qualification updates and TrendForce price prints; this sleeve should be paired against memory beta (e.g., MU) or nearline HDD exposure if you want a purer eSSD bet. For risk control, add hedges keyed to hyperscaler capex dispersion and to China NAND supply headlines. The main signposts we will monitor weekly are: 1) TrendForce contract price updates and channel commentary on bit‑to‑price tradeoffs, 2) SanDisk’s BiCS8 mix and explicit disclosure of start‑up/underutilization as they trend toward zero, 3) evidence that 256TB qualifications are expanding beyond 1–2 anchor customers, 4) any incremental YMTC or Korean supply announcements that change 2026 bit growth math, and 5) progress toward HBF specification milestones alongside any evidence of early silicon in 2H26. If these line up as management and the street expect, the risk‑reward skews positively; if pricing momentum stalls while YMTC accelerates, or if enterprise SSD timelines slip, the positioning should be cut back toward a neutral, consumer‑and‑client‑only cycle capture.  ￼

Key source triangulation supporting this analysis includes: Wells Fargo’s detailed bridge from underutilization/start‑up costs to FY26 gross margin drivers and its reminder that SanDisk receives ~40% of JV bits from Yokkaichi/Kitakami while owning ~49% of the JV, alongside explicit BiCS8 mix targets and eSSD qualification disclosure; Mizuho’s call‑outs on pricing, allocation, GB300 qualification and valuation context; Barclays’ equal‑weight stance and margin cadence; GF Securities’ “HBM moment” thesis with 2026 supply/demand math and the observation that CSP eSSD orders have surprised procurement teams; TrendForce’s 3Q25 price increases and continuing tightness signals; Dell’Oro’s data‑center capex trajectory; and SanDisk’s own releases on UltraQLC and HBF including the FMS award and SK hynix standardization MOU. Together these paint a consistent picture of a tightening market, a cost/mix inflection in FY26, and a credible path for SanDisk to monetize both.  ￼  ￼  ￼  ￼  ￼  ￼  ￼

In sum, this is a cyclical upturn with company‑specific torque. The base case is that pricing stays firm into 2026, BiCS8 mix ramps to ~45%, enterprise SSD qualifications broaden, gross margin steps into the low‑to‑mid‑30s% band, and free cash flow compounds. The bull case layers on faster eSSD adoption at 128TB/256TB densities as AI data lakes proliferate and HBF progress catalyzes a new conversation about SanDisk’s role in the memory hierarchy. The bear case is a 2026 capex digestion coinciding with supply additions and a longer BiCS8 learning curve, which would cap margins below 30% and defer the re‑rating. Position accordingly, keep the catalysts tight, and let the pricing and qualification tape tell you when to add or take down risk.  ￼

ㅡㅡㅡㅡㅡㅡㅡ
Citi) 반도체: 
겨울이 끝나고, 봄이 오고 있습니다.

요약: 우리는 2025년 예상 DRAM 수요/공급(S/D) 비율이 -1.0%로 개선되고, 2025년 예상 NAND 수요/공급(S/D) 비율은 +0.3%로 안정화될 것으로 예상하고 있습니다. 

이는 메모리 수요의 분리(decoupling)에 크게 기인합니다. 
2025년 1분기에는 단기적으로 가격 조정이 있을 가능성이 높지만, 2025년 2분기부터는 서버 DDR5 수요 회복, 차세대 HBM의 가격 프리미엄, 공급업체들의 제한적인 투자(capex) 전략에 힘입어 메모리 가격이 하락세에서 벗어나기 시작할 것으로 전망합니다. 

따라서 DRAM과 NAND의 평균판매가격(ASP)이 각각 2025년 2분기 및 3분기부터 예상보다 빠르게 회복될 것이라는 긍정적인 전망을 유지하고 있습니다. 

SK하이닉스, 마이크론, 삼성전자의 매수(Buy) 의견을 재확인합니다.

1. 2025년 DRAM 수요/공급(S/D) 비율 -1.0%
2025년 DRAM 산업의 S/D 비율이 -1.0%로 개선될 것으로 예상하며, 이는 AI 관련 애플리케이션의 수요 증가에 의해 주도될 것으로 봅니다. 우리는 2025년 동안 글로벌 DRAM 수요가 공급보다 더 빠르게 성장할 것으로 전망하며, 연간 수요는 전년 대비 +15.0% 증가하고 공급은 +13.9% 증가할 것으로 예상합니다. 애플리케이션별로 보면 DRAM 수요 회복은 주로 서버에서 발생하며, 서버 DRAM 수요는 2025년 전년 대비 +30.4% 증가할 것으로 예상되는 반면, 기존 PC/모듈 수요는 전년 대비 -15.6% 감소할 것으로 내다봅니다. 평균판매가격(ASP) 측면에서 2025년 DRAM의 연간 혼합 ASP는 전년 대비 +15% 증가할 것으로 예상하며, 이는 이전 전망치(+12%)보다 상승한 수치입니다. 분기별로는 1분기 2025년 DRAM ASP가 전분기 대비 -7% 감소할 것으로 예상되나, 2분기 +1%, 3분기 +7%, 4분기 +13%로 반등할 것으로 보이며, 이는 서버 DRAM 및 HBM 제품군의 혼합 개선에 의해 견인될 것입니다.

2. 2025년 NAND 수요/공급(S/D) 비율 +0.3%
2025년 NAND 산업의 S/D 비율은 +0.3%로 균형을 유지할 것으로 예상됩니다. NAND S/D 긴축은 2025년 2분기까지 약간 완화되겠지만, 3분기에는 다시 긴축된 균형을 이루게 될 것으로 전망됩니다. 우리는 2025년 NAND 비트 공급이 전년 대비 +9.8% 증가하고, NAND 비트 수요가 전년 대비 +9.4% 증가할 것으로 예상합니다. SSD 수요는 2025년 462.4억 개(+7.0% YoY)로 성장할 것으로 보며, eSSD 출하량(+6.8% YoY, 4,600만 개)과 박스당 용량(+19.1% YoY, 5,051GB)이 클라이언트 SSD 성장 둔화를 상쇄할 것으로 예상됩니다. 우리는 2025년 혼합 NAND ASP 성장률이 전년 대비 -6%로 개선될 것으로 보며(이전 전망 -8%), 분기별로는 1분기 -9%, 2분기 -3% 하락 후, 3분기와 4분기에 각각 +1%, +5% 상승할 것으로 전망합니다.

3. 메모리 투자비용(Capex) 2025년 전년 대비 +6.1%
글로벌 메모리 투자비용은 2024년 +14.2%에 이어 2025년에는 전년 대비 +6.1% 증가하여 총 413억 달러에 이를 것으로 예상됩니다. 2025년 투자비용은 주로 HBM 및 고급 DRAM에 집중될 것으로 보이며, 글로벌 DRAM 투자비용은 전년 대비 +14.8% 증가할 것으로 예상되는 반면, NAND 투자비용은 -6.8% 감소할 것으로 전망됩니다.

4. 주요 메모리 기업 매수 의견 유지
SK하이닉스, 마이크론(Christopher Danely가 분석 담당) 및 삼성전자에 대해 매수(Buy) 의견을 재확인합니다. 우리는 주요 글로벌 메모리 제조업체들이 제한된 메모리 공급 증가와 GPU 및 ASIC 기반 AI HBM 수요 증가로 2025년에 큰 혜택을 받을 것으로 예상합니다.

1분기 중반부터의 긍정적 모멘텀을 이어서 리서치팀은 이제 2분기 일반 메모리(DRAM 및 NAND 모두)의 가격 하락 폭이 전 분기 대비 기존의 한 자릿수 고대 (HSDs-%)에서 한 자릿수 저대(LSDs-%)로 축소될 것으로 예상하며,

하이닉스

SK하이닉스, 목표주가 36만원으로 상향 (JPM)

 1. 투자의견과 목표주가

 • 투자의견은 Overweight 유지

 • 목표주가를 기존 285,000원에서 360,000원으로 상향 조정 

 2. HBM 시장 내 리더십 지속

 • 경쟁사 대비 조기 대응(HBM4 샘플을 3월 NVIDIA에 선제 공급)

 • 독점적 소재 계약 등으로 기술 격차 유지

 • 경쟁사들의 인증 지연으로 HBM4 시장 점유율 확대 예상 (2026년 기준 37% 생산 비중 예상)

 3. HBM 매출 비중 확대에 따른 구조적 ASP 상승

 • 2026년 이후 HBM 매출 비중 50% 이상 전망

 • HBM4 ASP는 HBM3E 대비 35% 프리미엄 구조

 • HBM 중심으로 수익성이 높은 구조로 전환, 향후 4년간 이례적 실적 업사이클 전망

 4. AI 생태계와의 연계 강화

 • TSMC와의 로직 다이 협력으로 HBM4/4E 성능 경쟁력 강화

 • ASIC 시장 성장과 연계해 수혜 기대

 5. HBM 사업의 경제성

 • HBM 웨이퍼 단가 $22,000 수준, DRAM 대비 약 3배

 • 1만장/월 투자시 연간 매출 26억 달러 창출 가능

 • OPM은 60% 이상 수준 유지 전망

 6. 2024~2027년 실적 업사이클

 • 2025~2027년까지 4년 연속 영업이익 증가 전망 (2023년 적자 이후 회복)

 • 2025E EPS 43,005원 → 2026E 47,632원 → 2027E 63,591원

 • ROE 2025E 35.2%, 2026E 28.7%, 2027E 28.9%

 7. DRAM ASP 상승 및 비중 확대

 • 2025~2026년 DRAM ASP 증가세 유지 (2025E $4.4 → 2026E $5.0 → 2027E $5.9)

 • DRAM 매출이 전체 매출의 75~84% 차지, 영업이익 기여도 96~97% 수준

 8. NAND 부문 회복 속도는 제한적

 • 경쟁 심화 및 eSSD 가격 회복 지연으로 수익성 제한

 • NAND 영업이익률은 한 자릿수로 머물며 구조적 개선에는 시간 소요 예상

 9. 2025년 2분기 실적 프리뷰

 • 매출 19.9조원, 영업이익 9.0조원 전망 (OPM 45%)

 • DRAM ASP는 QoQ 2% 상승 전망, NAND는 여전히 약세

 • 실적은 전반적으로 컨센서스 부합 예상

 10. 주가 리레이팅 근거

 • HBM 중심의 구조적 수익성 개선과 예측 가능한 AI 수요에 기반한 실적 가시성 향상

 • 메모리 사이클의 축소 가능성과 AI 수요 기반 ASP 사이클로의 전환 기대

 • HBM 기술력에 기반한 프리미엄 적용 (P/B 1.9x, 업사이클 밸류에이션 적용)

 11. 재무 안정성 및 현금 흐름

 • 2025~2027년 FCFF는 각각 1.2조원, 2.4조원, 3.0조원 수준 예상

 • 2026년 이후 순현금 전환 전망 (2027년 순현금 5.2조원)

SK하이닉스(000660)
BUY/TP 325,000(유지/유지)
HBM3e 12단의 실적 개선 효과는 확인하고 판단하자

■ 투자포인트 및 결론
- SK하이닉스에 대해 6개월 목표주가 325,000원 (25년 예상 지배주주 BPS에 Target P/B 2.3배 적용)에 투자의견 매수를 유지. 동사의 2분기 매출액과 영업이익은 추정치를 각각 11.6%, 2.3% 상회하는 22.2조원과 9.2조원의 Earnings Surprise를 기록. 특히, 매출액이 추정치를 크게 상회한 이유는 DRAM과 NAND Bit Growth가 관세 부과 전 Pull In 수요에 힘입어 25.1%, 71%를 기록하였기 때문. 3분기에는 이와 같은 수요가 둔화되면서 DRAM과 NAND Bit Growth는 각각 2.7%, 0.5%를 기록할 것으로 예상. 다만, Blackwell향 HBM3e 출하량에 힘입어 DRAM Blended ASP가 QoQ로 10.1% 상승하면서 수익성은 개선될 것으로 예상되며, 3분기 매출액과 영업이익은 QoQ로 각각 5.6%, 16.7% 증가한 23.5조원과 10.7조원을 기록하면서 사상 최고 행진을 이어갈 것으로 예상. 특히, 내년 1분기부터 HBM3e 12단 제품이 Blackwell Ultra 제품에 본격적으로 탑재되면서 2025년에도 실적 개선 흐름은 이어질 것으로 보임. 이에 따라 2025년과 2026년 영업이익을 전망을 기존대비 각각 2.2%, 23.2% 상향한 39.6조원과 53.9조원으로 상향. Blackwell Ultra의 경우 주요 Sovereign AI, Stargate 2차 Project, GPU as a Service 업체들의 수요가 클 것으로 예상

■ 주요이슈 및 실적전망
- DRAM 시장에서 존재감이 커지고 있는 CXMT는 올해 미국의 Blacklist로 선정되면서 외산 장비 수입에 어려움이 클 것으로 예상되며, 올해 연말 Wafer Capa도 기존 월 300K에서 260K로 감소 예상. 또한, 중국 AI반도체 업체들의 요구로 현재 HBM3를 개발하고 있는 것으로 추정되며, HBM의 낮은 수율과 범용 DRAM대비 Wafer 잠식 효과를 감안할 때 CXMT의 HBM개발 확대는 중장기적으로 범용 DRAM 수급에 긍정적인 영향을 미칠 것으로 예상

■ 주가전망 및 Valuation
- HBM 12단 시대가 2026년부터 본격적으로 형성될 경우 수율 문제 등을 고려할 때 HBM3e 가격 하락 속도는 시장 우려보다 완만할 것으로 예상되며 Content 증가에 따른 규모의 경제 효과의 확인이 필요해 보임. 여전히 Buy & Hold 전략 유효

메모리 4년 슈퍼사이클 진입 (JPM)

1. 글로벌 메모리 사이클

 • 데이터센터·AI 연산수요 급증으로 24~27년까지 4년짜리 메모리 업사이클 전망

 • 글로벌 메모리 TAM을 기존 대비 6~24% 상향

 • HBM4E 도입으로 Rubin Ultra GPU에서 기존 대비 4배 메모리 컨텐츠 증가

2. HBM 전망

 • 26년 HBM3E는 공급 과잉으로 가격 하락 압력, 그러나 HBM4는 공급 제한으로 35% 가격 프리미엄 가능

 • HBM4 TAM은 27년 900억 달러 규모로 가속 성장

 • 하이닉스는 고객 샘플 조기 출하로 HBM4 자격 획득에서 선두, 삼성·마이크론은 40% 미만 MS 경쟁 전망

 • Rubin Ultra에서 HBM 수요 급증 → 4배 컨텐츠 증가로 가격·TAM 성장 동시 발생

3. DRAM

 • 24~27년 사상 첫 4년 연속 가격 사이클 상승 예상

 • HBM이 DRAM TAM의 43% 차지(27년) → 가격 변동성을 줄이고 마진 하방 방어

 • SOCAMM2, GDDR7 등 신규 응용 확산으로 DRAM 수요 다변화

 • DRAM TAM 27년까지 연평균 27% 성장

4. NAND

 • 2년간 투자 부족, HDD 공급 부족 → eSSD 채택 확대

 • 26년까지 NAND ASP +7% 예상, 하지만 구조적 AI 스토리지 필수재로 보기는 아직 조심스러움

5. 밸류에이션

 • 주가는 1~2개월새 과거 고점 돌파

 • 현재 밸류, 과거 사이클 고점 수준이지만 구조적으로 마진 개선된 국면이라 단순 밸류 비교 부적절

 • 톱픽 순위: 하이닉스 > 삼성전자 > Nanya 

6. CapEx 및 기술 트렌드

 • 수요 급증 대응 위해 26~27년 메모리 Capex 7~12% 증가 예상

 • HBM 우선순위로 DRAM 투자 집중, NAND는 가동률 개선 및 점진적 전환 투자

 • 27년 이후 HBM5 세대부터 하이브리드 본딩 본격 도입 전망 → 주요 장비 업체 수혜

"See bar, clear bar… though post-market reaction confirms expectations were high; maintain Buy, PT to $145"

-- Target Price Methodology:

Our $145 price target is ~12x our calendar 2026 EPS of ~$12, slightly above its average forward P/E of 11x over the prior 12 months. For comparison, in the prior upcycle investors paid 10-11x peak 4-qtr EPS of >$9. 

We expect Micron to outgrow/earn the prior peak in the ensuing upcycle, and to the degree the company executes and an increasing portion of the growth is AI/HBM-driven, we expect willingness to pay improved multiples.

-- Risks to our target price include:

(1) Harder economic landing scenario materializes
(2) Actions to control supply reversed too early
(3) Memory demand remains weaker than anticipated for longer, driving sustained losses
(4) Irrational investment and price competition from established players in DRAM/NAND
(5) New entrants in DRAM/NAND gain traction
(6) Delays/issues delivering on technology/manufacturing roadmaps leads to market share loss
(7) New AI-driven HBM enters digestion period, and/or Micron struggles to drive adoption of its product

"HBM and Mobile Recovery Help Drive a Solid Quarter"

Raymond James has an 'Outperform' rating on MU with a $150 price target.

"Micron’s F3Q results and F4Q outlook were both better than consensus. Gross margins were ahead of our recent expectations, and are on track for further expansion in F4Q and FQ1 driven by pricing and mix tailwinds. 

HBM revenue grew ~50% q/q once again, and management now sees the possibility of achieving its year-end share target one quarter earlier. HBM4 roadmap looks solid, which could unlock further share gains in 2026.

While potential consumer pull-ins and tariffs present some risk, we expect current DRAM up-cycle to extend well into 2026 on GenAI/HBM strength (and iPhone 17 content increase). 

At 2.9x P/B, valuation is above prior peaks but is justified in our view given the secular HBM growth (on track to account for a third of DRAM sales in CY26). We raise estimates and target price from $120 to $150, and reiterate our Outperform rating.

-- Valuation Methodology:

Our valuation methodology for Micron Technology is based on P/B multiple comparisons to its historical average range and peer valuation.

-- General Risk Factors:

Following are some general risk factors that pertain to the businesses of the subject companies and the projected target prices and recommendations included on Raymond James research: 

(1) Industry fundamentals with respect to customer demand or product/service pricing could change and adversely impact expected revenues and earnings; 
(2) issues relating to major competitors or market shares or new product expectations could change investor attitude toward the sector or this stock; 
(3) Unforeseen developments with respect to the management, financial condition or accounting policies or practices could alter the prospective valuation.

While the memory market has enjoyed a period of relatively stable supply amid a healthy demand environment – supporting favorable pricing trends – the market has historically been subject to significant swings of supply/demand imbalance. 

Following recent industry consolidation, we believe risks related to potential oversupply (with corresponding pricing collapse) have been largely mitigated given rational behavior among the remaining suppliers, and limited investment in capacity expansion (capex has largely been technology-driven rather than capacity-driven).

"$120B WFE in '25 and '26; AMAT PT to $240, LRCX PT to $110, & KLAC PT to $1,000"

Needham has a 'Buy' rating on AMAT with a $240 price target.

Needham's summary statement regarding AMAT in the report includes the following:

"We are revising up our WFE estimates to $120B and $120B in '25 and '26, and adjusting our MSI estimates lower for 2025 and 2026, despite still seeing 8% MSI growth next year. Excluding part of China WFE that is closed for U.S. semicap companies, we see adjusted WFE to be $110B and $108B in '25 and '26. We think the market is underestimating 2025 WFE by about 10%.

We are seeing WFE mix to change next year. Foundry/logic WFE is likely flat, as accessible China WFE decline in '26 remains a drag. DRAM WFE, which no longer has a China element due to CXMT shadow ban, is likely up in double digits next year, mostly driven by HBM. NAND WFE, however, could be flat to down next year as the recovery of NAND market remains underwhelming.

Still, we are bullish on semicap. AI has fundamentally changed semis, but there is still some distance between AI and semicap (except a handful of advanced packaging names). We believe 2026 is likely the inflection point, when general semicap will start to be the real AI beneficiary. We think the AI benefit will first move the semicap needle in DRAM next year, and then in leading-edge foundry in 2027.

The setup into 2H25 appears to be more favorable to AMAT than KLAC and LRCX. We think the market is at peak bearishness on AMAT, as AMAT's valuation discount to SOX is at a level unseen since September 2020. We think DRAM inflecting higher next year is a tailwind for AMAT, as DRAM remains the most market-share accretive segment for AMAT and its strength should lead to AMAT outperformance. 

The name has been marred by China underperformance and share loss narrative this year, neither of which we consider as fair and substantiated. 

With this note, we are raising AMAT PT to $240 and favor the name over KLAC and LRCX. We are not giving up on KLAC and LRCX yet. We are raising KLAC PT to $1,000 and LRCX PT to $110. We think as the market comes to terms of "semicap is AI beneficiary", the rising tide should lift all boats. Nevertheless, we think the setup is the most favorable for AMAT from here.

최근 미국의 관세 정책에 대한 우려로 서버 수요가 회복세를 보이며, 평균판매가격(ASP)의 흐름도 예상보다 긍정적입니다. 실제로 가격 반등은 2025년 하반기 NAND ASP의 반등 기대감을 높였고, 이에 따라 시장 심리도 점차 긍정적으로 전환되며 투자자 신뢰가 회복되고 있습니다.

메모리 산업의 최신 동향에 대해 다이와 캐피탈은, 고객사들이 재고 조정을 계속하고 있음에도 불구하고 전반적인 가격 환경이 하락세에 머무는 가운데, 중국 정부의 구형 DRAM 보조금 정책에 힘입어 스마트폰 및 PC용 범용 메모리 수요가 개선되고 있다고 분석했습니다.

HBM 수요는 강세… NVIDIA B300 출시 지연 우려도
고대역폭 메모리(HBM) 관련해서는, NVIDIA 등 주요 고객의 수요 전망에는 큰 변화가 없지만, HBM3E 12H가 적용된 B300 플랫폼의 출시 지연 우려로 인해 2025년 수요 전망에 다소 영향이 있을 수 있다고 전했습니다.

중국 브랜드 영향은 제한적… 산업 구도 변화 크지 않아
또한, NVIDIA가 2025년 하반기까지 메모리 공급업체들에 HBM4 인증 및 공급 완료를 요청했지만, 다이와 캐피탈 조사에 따르면 루빈(Rubin) 플랫폼은 2026년 하반기로 출시가 지연될 가능성이 있어 HBM3E 12H의 제품 수명이 2026년 상반기까지 이어질 것으로 전망했습니다. 이로 인해 후속 수요도 기대할 수 있는 상황입니다.

한편, 중국 업체들의 DRAM 시장 진입에 대해서는, DDR4 및 DDR5 공급 증가에 대한 우려가 존재하지만, 중국 업체들은 공정 기술 및 성능 면에서 글로벌 선도 기업들과 격차가 커 단기적으로는 시장에 미치는 영향이 제한적일 것이라 보았습니다.

특히 주목할 점은, 삼성이 2025년 1분기부터 HBM3E 12H 성능 향상을 위한 재설계에 착수했으며, 2분기 내 공정 인증을 진행할 계획이라는 것입니다. 하지만 NVIDIA 차세대 플랫폼 출시가 지연되면서, 2025년 HBM3E 12H 수요는 시장 기대치에 못 미칠 가능성도 언급됐습니다. 반면, 마이크론(Micron)은 HBM 생산능력 확장을 적극적으로 추진 중이며, 전반적인 산업 구조에는 큰 변화가 없을 것으로 다이와 캐피탈은 분석했습니다.

The new wave of computing demand driven by generative AI and large language models (LLMs) is pushing up the entire global memory market. At the same time, major traditional hard disk drive (HDD) manufacturers have begun cutting production, which could result in at least six months of supply shortages. This is likely to redirect some orders toward SSDs, further tightening the NAND supply chain. Most industry players believe memory price hikes in Q4 are already a certainty. Although October contract prices have yet to be finalized, upstream producers are taking a stronger stance on increases, and the magnitude could exceed earlier estimates.

Specifically, DDR5 contract prices were originally projected to rise by 10–15% and spot prices by 15–25%, but there is now room for upward revisions. DDR4 is also expected to see contract prices rise more than 10% and spot prices more than 15%. The market has been quick to respond. Phison, a major NAND controller chip manufacturer, recently resumed partial price quoting and directly raised prices by about 10%, seen as a signal of a rising NAND Flash market. Memory giant Micron’s latest earnings report also noted that AI demand is spreading across data centers, PCs, smartphones, and automotive applications, laying the foundation for growth in 2026.

Global server shipments in 2025 are projected to grow 10% year over year, a significant upward revision from previous forecasts. Demand for AI servers is the strongest, also helping to revive traditional server demand. The adoption of AI technology in product design and manufacturing has boosted productivity by 30–40%, increased wafer image analysis volume fivefold year over year, shortened R&D cycles, and improved yields.

The PC market is seeing stronger demand, driven by the retirement of Windows 10 and the rise of AI PCs. Smartphones are following the high-capacity trend, with one-third of flagship models now equipped with 12GB or more of DRAM.

In the automotive sector, ADAS (advanced driver-assistance systems) and AI-powered in-cabin experiences are requiring more memory, fueling demand for high-performance DDR5 and LPDDR5. Robotics, drones, and AR/VR are also emerging as new growth engines in the embedded market.

Industry insiders point out that AI is expanding from data centers into personal devices and automobiles, broadly driving up memory demand. With the ongoing ramp-up of AI server shipments, the high-capacity trend in PCs and smartphones, and the rapid growth of automotive and embedded markets, the global memory industry is entering a new phase of structural growth.

SK hynix

[Mirae Asset Securities – Semiconductor Analyst: Kim Young-Gun]

General-Purpose Memory Market Under Pressure, but Upgrade in Rating

We upgrade our investment rating on SK hynix from Neutral → Buy, and raise our target price to ₩520,000 (from ₩300,000) — an increase of 73%.
Our 2026 operating profit estimate rises to ₩59.8 trillion (from ₩45.9 trillion), and our target P/B multiple increases to 2.5× (from 1.7×), up 30.5% and 47.0%, respectively.
We judge that the rebound in the general-purpose memory market has come earlier and stronger than we previously expected.
For FY2026, we estimate DRAM bit growth at +18.7% and ASP growth at +12.3% (general-purpose DRAM +32.6%, HBM –8%).
Unlike our previous view — which capped the target P/B multiple at 1.7× due to intensifying HBM competition — we now believe the strength in conventional DRAM pricing may exert downward resistance on HBM price declines.
Accordingly, we raise the target multiple to 2.5×, in line with Micron’s valuation level.
Limited Supply but Sustained Demand Heading into 2026

Since early October, the 2026 server shipment forecast has been revised up repeatedly to +4.0% YoY (from +2.0% → +3.3%), reflecting installations at new data centers being completed in North America and China.
In contrast, demand for smartphones and PCs remains sluggish, with 2026 forecasts revised downward to +0.4% YoY (MoM –0.3 ppt) and +1.1% YoY (MoM –1.5 ppt), respectively.
Amid weak consumer demand, memory wafer capacity expansion remains limited. As HBM3E transitions to HBM4, the capacity conversion ratio from conventional DRAM to HBM is expected to expand by 30%, tightening overall supply.

In storage, the HDD market — now an oligopoly of three major suppliers — faces supply disruptions, as it struggles to migrate beyond 60 TB-class high-capacity drives.

At present, contract prices for both DRAM and NAND are expected to rise sequentially by ~5% QoQ through 4Q 2026.
However, since this is only the current projection, buyers are more likely to concentrate purchases during short-term price dips rather than base procurement on mid- to long-term forecasts.
Some buyers are reportedly accepting NCNR (No Cancel / No Return) conditions.

Will General-Purpose DRAM Prices Stabilize in 2H 2026?

There appear to be three major variables that could influence the outcome:

Adoption of LPDDR5X SO-CAMM by NVIDIA’s Vera CPU, driving competition for demand with the mobile segment.

Rising GDDR7 demand with the launch of NVIDIA’s CPX platform.
Consumer demand recovery, led by the end of Windows 10 extended support (1-year grace period) and the launch of the foldable iPhone.

Memory Shortage Crisis! Major Clients Only Receiving 70% of Orders as Server DRAM Prices Surge 50%

$MU, SK hynix, Samsung

As major global memory manufacturers finalize their Q4 2025 contract prices, reports indicate that even top U.S. and Chinese customers are receiving only about 70% of their requested orders, while server DRAM contract prices have skyrocketed by as much as 50%. Due to production capacity being heavily prioritized for select clients, lower-tier customers may see their supply fulfillment rates drop below 40% over the next two quarters.

The explosive growth in AI demand has triggered severe shortages and rapid price hikes across the entire memory industry. According to supply chain sources, the market began to “shift dramatically” in Q3, and it’s now nearly impossible to secure supply. Many memory module makers are facing a “no inventory” crisis in October. Korean giants have reportedly stopped even quoting DDR5 DRAM prices, as their inventories are completely depleted. New orders are being delayed until November.

Industry insiders warn that “it’s not just October — securing inventory will remain difficult throughout Q4,” adding that urgent orders must be purchased at spot prices.

In the spot market, DDR5 prices have surged sharply since late September. Prices for 16Gb DDR5 chips, which were around $7–8 in September, have now jumped to about $13, with further increases expected.

Samsung Electronics recently set its Q4 contract prices, with server DRAM seeing the sharpest rise, driven by strong server demand and the company’s shift to advanced manufacturing nodes. Enterprise SSDs rose 15–35%, while server RDIMMs climbed 40–50%, far above the industry’s earlier expectation of a 30% increase.

Despite these price hikes, supply shortages continue to worsen. Both U.S. and Chinese cloud service providers (CSPs) are reportedly receiving only about 70% of their orders, based on average shipment volumes from the first three quarters of 2025.

The situation is particularly severe among the four major U.S. hyperscalers, which account for roughly 50% of global data center capacity. With OpenAI and Oracle planning to ramp up data center shipments in the second half of 2026, server memory shortages are expected to persist through the end of 2026.

Smaller firms, distributors, and memory module makers face even greater challenges. Because their delivery priorities rank far below those of large-scale clients, their average order fulfillment rates are just 35–40%. Industry participants expect the “no memory available” crisis to persist at least through Q1 2026.

Nanya Technology noted that DDR4 currently accounts for about 20% of the global DRAM market, with more than 10% being DDR4 or LPDDR4. While PC manufacturers are rapidly migrating to DDR5, TVs, networking, consumer devices, and industrial PCs (IPC) have been slower to transition. However, data center switches still rely heavily on DDR4, meaning that a 10% or greater supply gap could persist for another 1–2 years.

Industry experts warn that the memory shortage could evolve into a broader supply chain disruption. As PC makers transition to DDR5, contract prices are being raised continuously, OEM inventory levels are falling, and PC DRAM supply constraints are tightening further.

Although many companies front-loaded orders in early 2025 to hedge against tariff risks, a reduction in tariffs in 2026 could help economic recovery. However, even if PC demand rebounds, OEMs may struggle to secure sufficient volume, even at premium prices — potentially recreating “pandemic-era supply chain collapse” conditions.

A senior Xiaomi executive recently stated that memory chip costs have risen far beyond expectations, forcing price increases on new products and warning that cost pressures could intensify further — underscoring that the memory price surge and shortages are now spreading to the PC and smartphone industries.

post.text:
🏭 AI demand is pushing memory chips into a new supercycle,  and analysts pointing to a 2027 peak for this cycle.

Supplier DRAM inventory near 3.3 weeks, shows how little buffer memory chip makers have on hand. With so little supplier stock, even a small increase in demand or a disruption in production can cause big swings in pricing.

Spot pricing shows the squeeze already, with DDR4 8Gb at $6.35 and DDR5 16G at $7.535, both sitting near year highs.

Contract pricing is set to climb again with reports that Samsung and SK hynix are pushing additional increases with customers after Micron’s moves.

Tight supply comes from fabs shifting lines to HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) used in AI accelerators, which caps standard DRAM output even as server builds expand and upgrades roll forward.

Supplier selection adds pressure, with Samsung newly certified for Nvidia HBM3E and SK hynix still the main Nvidia HBM source, so near term allocation stays tight for general DRAM buyers.

Storage demand is reinforcing the move, since HDD shortfalls are steering data centers to nearline SSDs and expectations for NAND price hikes into Q4 are adding to server costs.

📦 U.S. trade officials are considering 2 possible policies that could directly hit chip imports.

The first is a 1:1 production rule, which would require companies to produce 1 chip in the U.S. for every 1 chip they import. That forces manufacturers to shift more fabrication capacity into the U.S., but in practice it is very hard, because most advanced chips are only made in Asia.

The second is a 100% tariff on imported chips. That doubles the price U.S. buyers would have to pay for any foreign-made chip. Since there is already a shortage of DRAM and HBM, U.S. companies cannot simply switch to local supply, because there isn’t enough of it. So the main effect would be higher costs for U.S. buyers, with no relief on supply.

In other words, both rules would make it more expensive to buy chips in the U.S. at a time when the market is already tight. The policies do not create new chips, they just change who pays more for them.

Broker views echo this setup, with Morgan Stanley guiding to a 2027 peak and KB Securities calling Samsung the biggest beneficiary thanks to the Pyeongtaek expansion that spans HBM, DRAM, and NAND capacity.

Deutsche initiation on Micron $MU

We are launching coverage of Micron (Ticker: MU) with Buy rating and $150 price  target.  We are constructive on both the cyclical and secular setup facing Micron.  On  the secular side, we believe High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is an underrated driver  of gen/gen AI processor performance improvements, and believe growth in HBM  bits and ASPs should drive DRAM revenue growth (~75% of MU revenues) and  profitability above historical levels.  We believe Micron will be a particular  beneficiary of this trend, with HBM revenues expected to rise to ~23% of sales by  CY26E (from ~0% in CY23), and HBM GMs well above corporate average (DBe  ~60%+, vs. non-HBM ~35%).  On the cyclical side, we see a path to continued bit  growth and ASP expansion in non-HBM DRAM in the coming years driven by higher  DRAM content-per-device as well as healthy supply-demand dynamics.  In NAND  (the remaining ~25% of MU revs) we are admittedly less optimistic, as we see fewer  content-per-application growth drivers than we do in DRAM, and view the supply- demand environment as less favorable.  All told, this constructive outlook leaves our  CY26 revenue/EPS estimates ~+3%/+8% above current Street estimates (DBe  $51.7b/$14.00), and we see a solid path to further positive revisions.  Despite the  YTD run for MU shares (MU +48% YTD vs. S&P +6%, SOX +13%), we view current  levels as still offering attractive upside, with shares on trading at ~9x P/E on what  we view to be conservative CY26E estimates.  Therefore, we base our $150 P/T on  ~11x our CY26E EPS of $14.00, in-line with the company’s 5-year median P/E  multiple.  Initiate coverage with a Buy rating
