post.text:
Interesting Deutsche expert call on the outlook in the HBM market with former SVP at Samsung who's now running a consulting firm => market bullishness on Samsung share gains and concerns around Micron's competitiveness due its HBM4 base die are overblown:

"We recently caught up briefly with Dr Harold Lee, founder and head consultant at  Itz Lee M Co, a consulting firm.  Prior to this, Dr Lee was SVP at Samsung, where he  was in charge of HBM, hybrid bonding, and 3D DRAM for future product  development. This  update follows two HBM expert calls in Dec 2024 and June 2024.

There has been much discussion of late around HBM4 at Nvidia with claims in the  Korean press ( here ) that the Samsung comeback was "on" regarding major share  recovery at HBM4, potentially rising to "up to 30%" in H2-26.  Based on what Dr Lee  has picked up from various sources, he notes that SK Hynix delivered its HBM4  samples to Nvidia in March, with completion of qualification likely next month.  By  contrast, Samsung delivered only a small amount of HBM4 samples in July, with  major samples likely delivered in September.  This puts Samsung six months behind  in terms of HBM4 ramp timing versus the leader, SK Hynix, and three months  behind Micron.  

While Samsung has had execution and yield issues some of which  will likely sustain into the HBM4/HBM4E era, Dr Lee notes that what favours  Samsung's long-term share recovery is the amount of potential clean room space  it can offer up to purchasers.  In the near term, Samsung offers capacity growth  potential via the Pyongtaek campus (P4 ramp ongoing, P5 in construction, P6) with  logic conversions on top, while in the longer term, there is a new site in Yongin (6  megafabs, from 2030).  By contrast, SK Hynix has its new campus in Yongin (4  megafabs), operational from May 2027, while Micron has its new fab in Idaho  (output to begin in 2027), followed by a new megafab in New York (2029+).

Dr Lee believes that the discussion around Nvidia wanting >10GBps pin speed (vs  8-10GBps in the JEDEC standard) to counter AMD competition is over-blown.  Samsung and Micron have said they have achieved 11Gbps, while SK Hynix has  said it is already above 10GBps.  In HBM4, the big change is that the number of I/Os  is doubled, which drives bandwidth, while the overall bandwidth per pin is  determined by two factors: circuit design in DDR5 and circuit design for the base  logic die.  On the base die, SK Hynix is working with TSMC (likely at 3nm finFET),  while Micron said it will maintain a conventional base die at HBM4, which was  perceived to be a concern.  Samsung meanwhile will use its own foundry process  (4nm logic).  However, using a 2xnm process for the base die is 'good enough' at  HBM4 in the expert's view, so this is not likely be a major driver of share shifts in his  view, even though Micron is likely to move to TSMC 3nm at HBM4E.  

A more  important question remains progression at Samsung on 1cnm yield (one  report  suggests it is nearly 80% while  another  points to 50%, but with variability).  While Micron has delivered improvements in the maturity of its packaging yield to  70% (from 30% a year ago) using its packaging method (TC-NCF), Dr Lee notes that  SK Hynix likely has an equivalent yield of over 90% by contrast.  As a result, even if  Micron's HBM gross margin has topped 60% using TC-NCF in recent quarters, SK  Hynix, in his view, is likely standing much higher using MR-MUF.  In addition, SK  Hynix's thermal dissipation remains an advantage.  Furthermore, going into higher  stacks, the gap between MR-MUF and TC-NCF is likely to widen again, while  Samsung still likely has lower packaging yields than Micron.

With die stacks trending to 16-hi at HBM4E for Rubin Ultra, higher stacks remain  then a key challenge for Samsung and Micron, despite TC-NCF yields improving  markedly.  Dr Lee notes then that ASMPT and K&S then have an opportunity to drive  fluxless TCB introduction to improve the TC-NCF process at both players.  This  would likely mean some new toolsets being required (not upgrades), while cleaning  the surface of the micro-bumps is very different.  SK Hynix by contrast has more  room to go with MR-MUF to scale up to 16-hi and potentially to 20-hi.  As a reminder,  SK Hynix only uses TCB for temporary bonding, so its usage is much lower.
As for hybrid bonding, Dr Lee remains relatively sceptical on hybrid bonding  insertion for HBM until 20-hi at the earliest (HBM5).  He notes using hybrid bonding  is still a delicate process because of several problems that have yet to be solved, while there is a significant increase in cost of production at this point, which could  lead to big challenges for the likes of Micron or Samsung if they introduce early at  16-hi (overall HBM packaging cost is ~2x in his view vs TCB)

Lastly, we discussed HBM4 share and pricing.  In Dr Lee's view, IF Samsung can  improve its yield to that of Micron, its HBM4 share should reach 10% by Q4-26,  which is lower than the "up to 30%" claim reported above.  However, on HBM3E, Dr  Lee expects the impact of a 30% discount from Samsung post its recent  qualification to drive HBM3 pricing down while this discount should allow  Samsung to gain 10-20% share at Nvidia on HBM3E, primarily on low-to-medium- end SKUs.  As for HBM4 pricing, Dr Lee notes that HBM4's premium over HBM3E  should be significant given a much higher production cost.  He hears that SK Hynix  is pricing HBM4 at 70% higher than HBM3E, at $23-24 per GB, compared with the  current price of HBM3E of below USD14 per GB (original HBM3E price was USD17  per GB).  The 40% increase on HBM4 vs HBM3E at start date reflects a 30% higher  die penalty (~2x conventional DRAM, going to 2.6x) with yields (higher stacks,  higher I/O pads) takes up the remaining delta.

We continue to view Micron as a strong beneficiary of growth trends in HBM, even  despite the multitude of bearish reports suggesting downside to market share and  pricing.  On HBM3E, we remain confident that Micron can maintain share in the 20- 25% range through 2026-2027, with Samsung’s incremental share likely to come  at the expense of SK Hynix rather than Micron.  While Samsung’s qualification on  HBM3E may have some drag on HBM3E 12-hi pricing (we model a 5% decline for  Micron for CY-26), we do not believe the impact to Micron will be as bad as feared,  or as bad as the impact on SK Hynix.  On HBM4, we are encouraged by the expert's  commentary on initial pricing, with his initial +70% estimate gen-on-gen growth  well above our assumptions (we model only +10% growth gen-on-gen, while some  buy-siders assume pricing could be down gen/gen pending market share/supply  dynamics).

For Micron, we believe earning higher market share in HBM4 will  remain a challenge especially with many of Samsung’s technical issues likely in the  rear-view mirror, but we believe recent fears over pin speeds are overblown, with  Micron’s base die likely to be sufficient until HBM4E.  In addition, on HBM4E, we  also believe that the number of qualified suppliers could decline given the higher  degree of customization of the base die, a potential opportunity for Micron.

While Samsung should relatively easily convert its existing front-end 1anm  capacity over to 1cnm (as well as packaging lines, C1 and C2, in Cheonan) to  support its HBM4 ramp, looking further out, we continue to believe that greenfield  HBM spending more broadly should be a key driver of strength in WFE spending in  2027-30, which provides a strong support of WFE growth.  Our Buy-rated names on  the front-end that are levered to this theme include ASML (EUR 870.10 ) , Lam  ($145.04 ) and ASMI(EUR 534).

As for the back-end, the commentary on the timing of hybrid bonding insertion  (primarily 20-hi) is still in line with what we assume for Besi (Buy; EUR 138.50), but  the potential for MR-MUF extension at SK Hynix into 20-hi remains a risk, as is slow  progress on improving hybrid bonding cost and yield.  On the test side, we continue  to like Technoprobe (Buy; EUR 8.83) on its potential to enter the HBM4 supply chain  with its vertical MEMS probe cards for singulated stack tests, and potentially later  on for DRAM wafer-level tests at HBM4E/5 with the introduction of high-speed (ie  known good die) tests & hybrid bonding."

모건 스탠리(J. 무어, 2025년 6월 20일)

이 회사는 마이크론의 AI 사업이 크게 성장하고 있으며, HBM과 LPDDR 수요가 평균 판매 가격(ASP)과 매출 총이익률 상승을 견인하고 있다고 언급했습니다. 밸류에이션이 낮지는 않지만, 지속적인 AI 배당을 고려하면 주가 상승 잠재력은 여전히 ​​높습니다.

- HBM과 LPDDR, AI 관련 매출 점유율 14%에서 30%로 끌어올리고, 매출총이익률 SK하이닉스와 수렴할 전망

마이크론의 AI 관련 사업이 빠르게 성장하고 있습니다. 

8월 분기 HBM 매출은 전 분기 대비 54% 증가한 20억 달러를 기록할 것으로 예상되며, LPDDR 및 eSSD 가격 또한 회복세를 보일 것으로 예상됩니다. 

AI 서버 수요는 고용량 DIMM 성장을 견인하고 있으며, 11월 분기 AI 매출 점유율은 30%까지 상승하여 전체 평균 판매가(ASP)가 약 30% 상승할 것으로 예상됩니다. 

SK하이닉스의 AI 매출 점유율은 이미 30%에 도달했으며, 매출 총이익률은 60%에 육박합니다. 마이크론은 향후 분기에 시장 상황이 수렴될 것으로 예상합니다.

- 소비재 및 NAND 드래그 요인 약화, 매출총이익률 개선 가속화 국면 진입

5월 분기 실적 전망에서는 소비자 제품과 NAND 가격 하락으로 인한 시장 우려가 제기되었습니다. 그러나 5월 분기부터 eSSD 물량 증가와 NAND 가격 상승이 맞물리면서 소비자 제품 비중이 크게 감소할 것으로 예상됩니다. NAND 가동률 상승으로 고정 비용이 희석될 것으로 예상되며, DDR4 현물 가격은 전년 동기 대비 150% 상승했습니다. 매출에서 차지하는 비중은 작지만 수익성에는 여전히 미미한 기여를 하고 있습니다.

- HBM 공급-수요 역학 변화 및 스마트폰 재고 변동으로 인한 위험

삼성은 여전히 ​​고사양 HBM 시장에서 어려움을 겪고 있으며, 이는 단기적으로는 마이크론에 유리합니다. 

그러나 삼성의 시장 점유율이 회복될 경우, 시장 이익률이 하락할 것입니다. 동시에, 아이폰과 같은 최종 고객의 조기 재고 축적은 2026년 초 일시적인 수요 감소로 이어질 수 있으며, 이는 재고 조정 위험에 대한 주의를 요합니다.

- AI는 명확한 논리로 DRAM을 구동하지만 자유 현금 흐름은 NVIDIA보다 여전히 약합니다.

AI 트렌드가 HBM 성장을 계속 견인할 것으로 예상되지만, 마이크론의 자본 지출은 여전히 ​​매출의 40%를 상회하여 주당 약 4달러의 잉여현금흐름을 기록하고 있는데, 

이는 엔비디아보다 훨씬 낮은 수치입니다. 

두 회사 모두 AI 열풍의 수혜를 입었지만, 엔비디아는 잉여현금흐름과 가치 평가 측면에서 더 매력적인 선택입니다.

post.text:
$MU

Morgan Stanley의 Micron Technology Inc.(MU)에 대한 수익 미리보기 보고서(2025년 6월 20일)에 따르면, 단기적으로 강세적인 전망을 뒷받침하는 세 가지 핵심 사항은 다음과 같습니다.  

1. 인공지능(AI) 사업의 급속한 성장: 마이크론은 AI 관련 사업(고대역폭 메모리 HBM, 저전력 LPDDR 등)에 대한 참여를 크게 늘렸으며, AI 수익 비중은 2월 분기 14%에서 11월 분기에는 약 30%로 증가할 것으로 예상됩니다. 

HBM 매출은 8월에 20억 달러에 도달할 것으로 예상되며, 이는 전년 대비 54% 증가한 수치로 전체 평균 판매 가격(ASP) 성장에 약 30% 기여할 것으로 예상됩니다. 

LPDDR 및 eSSD 수요는 AI 서버 및 데이터 센터의 성장과 함께 가속화되고 있으며, 3분기와 4분기에도 견조한 실적이 예상됩니다. 

회사의 사업 구조 조정을 통해 클라우드 사업의 성장이 더 투명해지고 투자자들의 관심을 끌게 될 것입니다.  

2. 매출 총이익률에 대한 압박이 감소합니다. 5월 분기의 매출 총이익률은 소비자 제품(스마트폰 등)과 NAND 시장의 영향으로 하락했지만, 이러한 부정적인 요인은 8월 이후 약화될 것입니다. 

eSSD와 NAND 시장 수요 회복, 가격 상승, 웨이퍼 용량 활용도 향상으로 매출 총이익률은 5월 37.0%에서 8월 43.9%로 증가할 것으로 예상됩니다(시장 컨센서스인 39.5%보다 높음). 

DDR4 가격 압박이 완화되면서 현물 가격은 전년 대비 150% 상승했습니다. 

매출에 미치는 영향은 제한적이었지만(약 10%), 전반적인 수익성에는 기여했습니다.  

3. 매력적인 가치 평가와 상승 여력: 현재 주가는 장부 가치의 약 3배로, 작년 최고치인 4배보다 낮고 이전 주기의 최고치인 2.7배에 가깝습니다. 

이는 아직 가치 평가가 너무 높지 않다는 것을 보여줍니다.

해당 기간 평균 주당순이익(EPS) 7달러를 기준으로 PER 14를 적용했습니다. 

AI에 대한 관심이 지속된다면 투자자들은 더 높은 밸류에이션 프리미엄을 부여할 가능성이 있습니다. 

2026 회계연도 주당순이익은 작년 최고치에 가까운 12~13달러에 이를 것으로 예상되며, 이는 주가의 추가 상승을 뒷받침할 것입니다.  

이 세 가지 주요 사항은 AI 기반 시장 수요, 수익 개선 및 가치 평가 잠재력 측면에서 마이크론의 우위를 보여주지만, 관세, 재고 및 경쟁 위험이 단기 실적에 영향을 미칠 수 있다는 점에 유의해야 합니다.

post.text:
$NVDA #skhynix

저는 deepseek dive의 느낌이 이제 없네요??

AI 칩 스케일업은 더 가속화되는듯

SK하이닉스, 목표주가 36만원으로 상향 조정 (JPM)

1. 투자의견 및 목표주가

- 투자 의견을 '과체중'으로 유지합니다.
- 목표주가를 285,000원에서 360,000원으로 상향 조정합니다.

2. HBM 시장에서의 지속적인 리더십

- 경쟁사 대비 선제적 대응 (3월 엔비디아에 HBM4 샘플 선공급)
- 독점적인 자재 계약을 통해 기술적 우위를 유지합니다.
- 경쟁사 인증 지연으로 HBM4 시장 점유율 확대 예상(2026년까지 생산 점유율 37% 예상)

3. HBM 매출 점유율 확대로 인한 구조적 ASP 상승

- 2026년 이후 HBM 매출 점유율이 50%를 넘어설 것으로 예상됩니다.
- HBM4 ASP는 HBM3E에 비해 35% 프리미엄 구조를 가지고 있습니다.
- HBM을 중심으로 한 고수익 구조로 전환, 향후 4년간 놀라운 수익 증가 예상.

4. AI 생태계와의 연계 강화

- TSMC와의 로직 다이 협업을 통해 HBM4/4E 성능 경쟁력을 강화합니다.
- ASIC 시장 성장과 함께 수혜가 예상됩니다.

5. HBM 사업의 경제성

- HBM 웨이퍼 비용은 약 22,000달러로 DRAM의 약 3배입니다.
- 한 달에 10,000개의 웨이퍼를 투자하면 연간 26억 달러의 수익을 창출할 수 있습니다.
- OPM (영업이익률)은 60% 이상을 유지할 것으로 예상된다.

6. 2024년부터 2027년까지 수익 증가

- 2025년부터 2027년까지 4년 연속 영업이익 증가 전망(2023년 적자 이후 회복)
- 2025년 예상 EPS: KRW 43,005 → 2026년 예상: KRW 47,632 → 2027년 예상: KRW 63,591.
- ROE: 2025년 예상 35.2%, 2026년 예상 28.7%, 2027년 예상 28.9%.

7. DRAM ASP 상승 및 점유율 확대

- DRAM ASP는 2025-2026년에도 계속 증가할 것으로 예상됩니다(2025년 예상 $4.4 → 2026년 예상 $5.0 → 2027년 예상 $5.9).
- DRAM 매출은 전체 매출의 75-84%를 차지하며, 영업이익에는 96-97%를 기여합니다.

8. NAND 세그먼트의 제한된 복구 속도

- 경쟁 심화와 eSSD 가격 회복 지연으로 수익성이 제한됨.
- NAND 영업이익률은 한 자릿수에 머무를 것으로 예상되며, 구조적 개선에는 시간이 걸릴 것으로 전망.

9. 2025년 2분기 실적 미리보기

- 매출 : 19.9조원, 영업이익 : 9.0조원 (OPM 45 %) .
- DRAM ASP는 전분기 대비 2% 증가할 것으로 예상되지만 NAND는 여전히 약세를 보일 것으로 전망됩니다.
- 전반적인 수익은 합의에 도달할 것으로 예상됩니다.

10. 재평가 정당성

- HBM 중심의 구조적 수익성 개선과 예측 가능한 AI 수요를 기반으로 수익 가시성이 향상되었습니다.
- 메모리 사이클이 단축되고 AI 수요 주도 ASP 사이클로 전환될 것으로 예상됩니다.
- HBM 기술 기반 프리미엄 적용(P/B 1.9배, 업사이클 가치평가 적용)

11. 재무 안정성 및 현금 흐름

- 2025년, 2026년, 2027년 FCFF (기업의 자유현금흐름)는 각각 1.2조원, 2.4조원, 3.0조원으로 전망됩니다.
- 2026년 이후 순현금화 전환 예상 (2027년 순현금 ​​5.2조원)

- SK hynix 憑藉 321 層 NAND 技術突破，瞄準 AI 數據中心熱潮  
  SK hynix 與數據存儲專家 Pure Storage 合作，優化四級單元（QLC）NAND 的性能和能效。QLC NAND 每單元可存儲 4 位數據，密度是單級單元（SLC）NAND 的四倍，非常適合 AI 工作負載中以讀取為主的使用場景，例如數據歸檔、備份和媒體存儲。

- 2025 年第一季度表現疲弱，但復甦跡象已現  
  SK hynix 的 NAND 部門在 2025 年第一季度表現不佳，收入僅為 3.175 萬億韓元，較 2024 年第一季度的 4.351 萬億韓元大幅下降，原因包括供應過剩和平均售價（ASP）季度同比下降 20%。然而，分析師預測，隨著 NVIDIA GB300 等 AI 服務器需求增加，企業級 SSD 價格可能在 2025 年第三季度上漲 10%。

- SK hynix 縮小與三星的 NAND 市場份額差距  
  SK hynix 的 NAND 市場份額從 2020 年的 11% 增長至 2024 年第四季度的 20.5%，與三星（33.9%）的差距縮小至 13.4 個百分點。這得益於 300 層 NAND 的量產以及 Solidigm 在 QLC 技術上的領先地位，使 SK hynix 能夠抓住 AI 驅動的存儲需求。

$TER earnings:

Teradyne reported a solid Q2 that beat the midpoint of its guidance, but the main story is the significant positive shift in outlook. The cautious tone from last quarter, which saw management withdraw full-year guidance due to trade uncertainty, has been replaced with confidence. Management now reports “improved visibility” and expects “AI will drive strong second half performance”.

The Q3 guidance confirms this inflection, calling for significant sequential acceleration with revenue guided up ~13.5% and non-GAAP EPS up ~37% at the midpoints. The recovery is being led by the Semiconductor Test group, where strengthening demand in Compute (SoC), Networking, and Memory is directly linked to AI applications. This confirms that the long-discussed secular drivers are now translating into near-term financial results.

Concerns from last quarter regarding memory digestion and broad end-market weakness appear to be reversing. Even the struggling Robotics division saw a sequential revenue improvement. While the beat-and-raise is encouraging, the results are still down year-over-year, indicating we are at the beginning of a cyclical recovery, not at a peak.

4. Themes, Drivers, and Concerns

The narrative has shifted dramatically from managing near-term uncertainty to executing on a tangible, AI-driven recovery.

Previous Themes & How They Evolved:

Near-Term Uncertainty: REVERSED. The primary concern from Q1 is gone. The CEO now cites “improved visibility” and expects a “strong second half,” a complete reversal from the guidance withdrawal last quarter.

Long-Term Secular Drivers: MATERIALIZING NOW. The thesis that AI, Compute, and Memory would drive growth is no longer a long-term story. The CEO explicitly named these as the drivers for the strong Q2 results and Q3 outlook.

Securing Strategic Wins: CONVERTING TO REVENUE. The strong outlook for Compute and Memory suggests that key wins highlighted last quarter (e.g., HBM4 performance test, Titan-HP for AI SLT) are beginning to ramp and contribute to revenue.

Previous Concerns & How They Evolved:

Robotics Division Struggles: PERSISTS, BUT IMPROVING. Robotics revenue grew 8.7% sequentially to $75M. While the macro backdrop may still be challenged, this is the first sign of a potential bottoming/recovery in the segment.

Memory Market Digestion: REVERSING. The Q1 concern of a “significant sequential decline” has flipped. The CEO now states “demand in… memory is strengthening,” signaling the digestion period is ending.

End Market Demand Weakness (Auto/Industrial): REVERSING/OFFSET. While the release gives no specific update on Auto/Industrial, the powerful recovery in Compute/Memory is more than offsetting any lingering weakness, leading to strong overall guidance.

Transitory Mobile Strength: MATERIALIZED. As predicted, mobile-driven strength from Q1 faded. Semi Test revenue declined sequentially. The growth engine has successfully shifted to AI/Compute.

Current Drivers:

AI Compute & Memory Test (SoC & HBM): This is the undisputed primary driver. The CEO stated SoC for AI was the “strongest growth driver” and that demand in compute, networking, and memory is strengthening. This is the core of the positive inflection.

Robotics Turnaround: The sequential growth in Robotics is a new, positive data point. If sustainable, it could provide a secondary growth lever.

5. Key Questions for the Earnings Call

Nature of the Recovery: Last quarter, visibility was “very limited.” Now, you’re guiding for a strong H2. What specifically changed in customer conversations, particularly around AI capacity, to give you this confidence? Is the Q3 ramp the start of the HBM4 design win translating to revenue?

Margin Trajectory: Your Q3 revenue guidance implies a strong >13% sequential growth. With this significant volume increase, should we expect non-GAAP gross margins to recover back towards the 59-60% level in Q3 and the second half?

Robotics Outlook: It was great to see robotics revenue grow to $75 million. Was this driven by shipments from the large automotive order you won last quarter, or are you seeing a broader-based recovery in the industrial automation market?

Mobile & Legacy Markets: The release rightly focuses on the AI-driven strength. Could you provide an updated outlook for the Mobile test market for the remainder of 2025? Are the Auto and Industrial end markets stabilizing, or still soft?

Capital Allocation: You repurchased $117M in stock in Q2. With visibility improving and a strong H2 outlook, should we expect you to accelerate repurchases towards the $1B authorization you announced last quarter?

The company shipped 2.2 million units of its latest generation ePMR drives, up from over 1.7 million last quarter. This mix shift pushed non-GAAP gross margin to 43.9%, a 260 bps sequential improvement and a 660 bps YoY expansion. 🟢 Aggressive Capital Returns Signal Confidence: After strengthening the balance sheet last quarter, WDC has pivoted aggressively to shareholder returns. It repurchased $553 million in stock, a huge increase from $149 million in the prior quarter. The company also announced a 25% increase in its quarterly dividend to $0.125 per share. This signals strong conviction in sustained, robust free cash flow generation ($599 million this quarter).

🟡 Underlying Cyclicality and Tariff Risk: While the current upcycle is powerful, the business remains cyclical by nature. This is a long-term risk to keep in mind. Broader macroeconomic risks, including potential tariffs, are also mentioned in the company’s forward-looking statements and remain a background concern.

🔴 Heavy Reliance on Cloud Persists: The company’s dependence on the Cloud segment has intensified. The Client and Consumer segments combined represent only 11% of revenue. While both showed some sequential improvement, their YoY growth is minimal (Client +5%) or negative (Consumer -1.2%). The company’s fortunes are almost entirely tied to the spending cycles of a few large hyperscale customers.

post.text:
A MUST READ INTERVIEW with a current Director at $MU on HBM & GPU/ASIC market ( $NVDA, $MU, Samsung struggles ):

1. The hyperscalers $AMZN, $MSFT, $GOOGL are achieving significantly higher GPU utilization rates than they had in the past years. In 2022 and 2023, the GPU utilization rates were less than 40% The ROI on that in terms of hyperscalers getting their investment back used to be 12-18months. Now, the utilization rates are 70%-80 %, and the ROI has accelerated to only 6-9 months.

2. When $NVDA's Rubin comes out, he expects even higher GPU utilization rates - 90%. With Blackwell next year, he expects the cost of training on hyperscalers to be in the $60-$70 per hour range and for inference, smaller cases to be in the $5-$10 per hour range.

3. The supply of $NVDA's H100 has dramatically increased. The shortage, in his view, has been reduced mostly because of $TSM, which has improved their 4nm yield a lot as the technology has matured and as HBM availability has been good. In his words, when it comes to HBM, we are now moving from »call scarcity« to »high-volume pricing«.

4. HBM has been almost 2X-2.5X year on year. Both SK Hynix as well as $MU first had yield challenges as the biggest problem is TSV technology (through-silicon via), because you have to put eight of these chips on top of each other. If you have to put 12 of these on top of each other the connection between them is the biggest challenge. Both $MU and SK Hynix have become very proficient in that area. He continues to see the pricing going up slightly on the ASP for HBM.

5. He gives the example of HBM use in B100. If you say eight-high stack, that's around $400-$500; if you're using five or six of those, that's around $2500-$ 3600. It is 30% of the GPU cost in most cases.

6. The reason why HBM capacity has caught up in his view is not because of Samsung, but because the TSV technology has matured, and both SK Hynix and $MU have converted most of their CapEx into expanding HBM. He thinks this year might be the last year where we have a scarcity. He thinks 2026 will be even better with availability.

7. The reason why Samsung has struggled with $NVDA's certification process is because of thermal issues. $NVDA B100 and H100 have very tight thermal margins because they're using more than 700W of power. Each signal requires eight Gbps per pin.

8. Samsung has been struggling with the DPPM rate (defect parts per million rate), as it is significantly higher on Samsung parts compared to their competitors. The second thing they struggle with is the eye diagram. The eye diagram is the margin, and according to him, that margin has always been poor compared to SK Hynix and $MU. The reason is that $NVDA uses NVLink. The poor margin also affects the data transfer.

9. According to him, it makes sense that $AVGO approved Samsung as they use less than 300W of power and have more margin, $AVGO uses four Gbps-six Gbps per pin, $NVDA uses twice that, both in power as well as data transfer rate.

10. He thinks that by 2028, $NVDA's market share will be reduced to 50-60% with most of it going to hyperscalers doing their own ASICs. He mentions $GOOGL, noting that their TPUs are at the forefront of this, as they have highly customized FP4 optimization for inferencing and have already deployed TPUs for Gemini, as well as for internal AI training. Second is $AMZN's with Trainium, while both $META and $MSFT are still a bit behind and need to catch up. If he had to make an educated guess, he thinks that $GOOGL and AWS are already serving 50% of their own internal inferencing with their custom ASICs.

2. HBM市場における継続的なリーダーシップ

- 競合他社に比べて積極的な対応（3 月に NVIDIA に HBM4 サンプルを先行供給）。
- 独占的な資材契約を通じて技術的優位性を維持します。
- 競合他社の認証遅延により、HBM4 の市場シェアが拡大すると予想されます (2026 年までに生産シェア 37% になると予想されます)。

3. HBM収益シェアの拡大による構造的なASP上昇

- HBM の収益シェアは 2026 年以降 50% を超えると予想されます。
- HBM4 ASP は、HBM3E と比較して 35% のプレミアム構造になっています。
- HBMを中心とする高収益体質に移行し、今後4年間は驚異的な収益回復が見込まれます。

4. AIエコシステムとの連携強化

- TSMCとのロジックダイ連携により、HBM4/4Eの性能競争力を強化。
- ASIC 市場の成長に伴い恩恵を受けることが期待されます。

- HBM ウェハの納品価格は約 22,000 ドルで、DRAM の約 3 倍です。

- 競争の激化と eSSD 価格回復の遅れにより収益性が制限されます。

久し振りに東京エレクトロン！や半導体解説

DDR4 8Gbスポット価格は6月だけで約2倍に急騰し、背景には中国CXMTがDDR4量産を段階的に停止しDDR5へシフトする計画がある。供給ひっ迫はメモリー各社のキャッシュフローを大きく改善し、すぐに装置・材料への設備投資意欲に火をつけるため、装置≫材料≫ガス・マスクの順で利益レバレッジが高い。
中でも東京エレクトロン（8035）はDRAMキャパシタのエッチング工程で実質独占状態にあり、FY25はDRAM向け売上が前年比+59%と装置各社で突出。価格高騰が続けば、同社が最も大きな増益インパクトを享受する公算が大きい。

背景

DDR4スポット価格: 主要8Gb品が6月前半だけで+50〜100%上昇、モジュールメーカーが在庫確保に奔走。
CXMTのDDR4撤退: 2025年末〜26年半ばにかけて量産ラインをDDR5へ置換、標準DDR4は最小限の継続にとどめる方針。
需給タイト化の波及: DRAM各社の営業CF改善→CapEx再開→装置・材料発注増という循環がスタート。

分野別インパクトと勝ち組候補

製造装置

東京エレクトロン (8035)
DRAM用新規装置売上がFY25に+59%増、HBM向けも取り込み構成比66%へ上昇。
DRAMキャパシタ用エッチ装置でシェア100%近く、投資再開の最上流で利益率28.7%。

SCREEN HD (7735)
シングルウエーハ洗浄装置シェア80%へ急伸、CY24に市場シェア「大幅改善」と自社開示。
洗浄工程は毎増産フェーズで必須、レバレッジ高。

アドバンテスト (6857)
高速DRAM／HBM対応T5801を2月発表、次世代DRAM量産テストに対応。
FY24はDRAMテスター需要けん引で売上7797億円・営業益29.3%。

シリコンウエーハ

SUMCO (3436)
300 mmウエーハで世界シェア約40%、AI・DRAM向けLTAで26年以降ASP上昇狙う。

信越化学 (4063)
24年1500億円投資で300 mm能力増強、25年度フル寄与見込み。

材料系

東京応化工業 (4186)
HBM用パッケージレジストの需要急増で材料セグメント構成比が上昇。

HOYA (7741)
フォトマスクブランクス極めて大きいシェアを長年維持（業界推定60〜70%）。

関東電化工業 (4047)
DRAM稼働率回復で特殊ガス販売増、FY24営業益+62億円。

どこが一番利益を得られるか？
最有力：東京エレクトロン (8035)
圧倒的DRAM依存度
DRAM向け新規装置が売上の6割強を占め、価格上昇→投資再開の直接恩恵が最大。

高い利益レバレッジ
装置売上は契約一件あたり数十〜数百億円規模で、営業利益率約29%。価格上昇がわずかでもCapExにつながれば利益跳ね返りが大きい。

競争優位性（実質独占）
DRAMキャパシタのエッチング工程は他社参入障壁が高く、値下げ競争が起こりにくい。

受注の可視性
メモリー市況回復時には顧客の前金発注比率が高く、キャッシュフロー改善が早い。

I’m keeping my eye on some mid-cap stocks this week—those sweet-spot companies with market caps between $2 billion and $10 billion that often get overlooked but can deliver big moves. The market’s been a rollercoaster lately, with large-caps like Tesla and Nvidia bouncing around and the S&P 500 down a couple percent year-to-date. I think mid-caps might be where the action’s at right now—less hype than small-caps, more growth juice than the big dogs. Here’s my watchlist and why I’m dialed in:

First up, Micron Technology ( $MU ). This one’s teetering on the edge of mid-cap territory with a market cap around $10 billion, give or take. I’m watching it because their earnings are coming up on March 20, and the buzz is already building. They’re deep in the memory chip game, which ties straight into the AI boom—everyone needs fast, efficient chips to power those models. I’ve noticed the stock’s trading at a pretty low forward P/E, maybe around 8 or 9, which screams undervalued to me when you consider how critical their tech is. This week, I’m looking for any pre-earnings chatter—maybe an analyst upgrade or supply chain news—that could nudge it up. If AI keeps dominating headlines, Micron could ride that wave early.

Next, CrowdStrike Holdings ( $CRWD ). They just dropped earnings last week on March 4, and the stock’s been a mover—up over 10% this year so far. Market cap’s hovering near $10 billion too, so it’s in that mid-cap zone. Cybersecurity’s a hot space, and CrowdStrike’s got a reputation for being a leader there. I’m watching this week because the post-earnings dust hasn’t fully settled—could be some profit-taking or a fresh rally if the market likes their outlook. Volatility’s high, which I love; it means there’s room for a swing either way. If tech sentiment holds up, I think this one’s got legs.

Then there’s Iovance Biotherapeutics ( $IOVA ). This biotech’s sitting at a market cap of about $2–$3 billion, and it’s one of those under-the-radar names I’m excited about. They’re working on cancer therapies—serious stuff with serious potential. I don’t have any inside scoop, but mid-March feels like a time when biotech could pop off with a clinical update or partnership news. I’m watching because the healthcare space has been quietly heating up in 2025, and a stock like this could double on the right catalyst. It’s risky, sure, but that’s why it’s on my radar—I like the upside.

Same vibe with Viking Therapeutics ( $VKTX ). Another biotech, probably in that $2–$10 billion range, and it’s all about obesity and metabolic disease treatments. I’ve been hearing whispers about their pipeline, and if anything drops this week—say, trial data or even a rumor of a big pharma tie-up—I think it could spike. Biotech’s a gamble, but mid-caps like Viking have that 10x potential over time if they hit the jackpot. I’m keeping tabs on it for any sudden volume spikes or chatter that might tip me off.

Finally, International Seaways ( $INSW ). This one’s a bit different—an energy shipping play with a market cap around $2–$3 billion. What’s got me interested is the crazy 15%+ dividend yield and a dirt-cheap P/E, maybe 3 or 4. Oil prices have been twitchy lately, and with all the tariff talk floating around, energy stocks could get a jolt this week. I’m watching to see if global demand news or geopolitical moves shake things up. It’s not sexy like tech, but I think it’s undervalued and could be a steady winner if energy holds firm.

Why mid-caps this week? Well, the broader market’s feeling shaky—large-caps are getting hammered by uncertainty, and small-caps are too wild for my taste right now. Mid-caps have historically done well in choppy times like this; they’ve got enough size to weather storms but still plenty of room to grow. I’m also thinking about what’s driving things—Fed comments from last week had the economy sounding “good,” but tariff threats and tech volatility are keeping everyone on edge. That’s where I see mid-caps stepping up, especially in sectors like tech, healthcare, and energy.

For me, it’s about spotting the catalysts. Micron’s got earnings hype, CrowdStrike’s riding momentum, Iovance and Viking could surprise with biotech breakthroughs, and International Seaways might just be a sleeper hit if oil ticks up. I’m not saying these are locks—markets are unpredictable as hell—but they’re on my screen because I think they’ve got the juice to move. If I had to pick one to dive deeper on, I’d lean toward Micron; that AI angle feels too big to ignore. 

What do you think—any of these catch your eye, or am I missing something in this mess of a market?

George.

post.text:
$LRCX Lam Research Corporation Earnings Call Key Highlights:

💰 Record Financial Performance and Margin Expansion
Lam Research reported March 2025 quarter revenue of $4.72 billion, up 8% sequentially, with gross margin reaching 49%—its highest since the Novellus merger. Operating margin hit 32.8%, and EPS came in at $1.04, all exceeding guidance midpoints. The June quarter guidance forecasts further improvement with revenue of $5 billion, gross margin of 49.5%, and EPS of $1.20, each near or at record levels for the company.
🏭 Foundry and NAND Lead Segment Growth
Foundry revenue reached a record high, representing 48% of system revenue, up from 35% in the prior quarter, driven by demand for gate-all-around (GAA) nodes and advanced packaging. NAND, accounting for 20% of system revenue, is expected to lead growth in the June quarter, propelled by technology conversions and strategic upgrades to enable stacking beyond 200 layers.

🚀 Momentum in New Products Across Etch and Deposition
Lam's Striker Spark ALD and ALTUS Halo systems continue to gain share, with the latter enabling 50% resistance reduction in 3D NAND interconnects. In etch, the Akara system is solidifying Lam’s market lead in conductor etch, with wins in both logic and NAND applications. These platforms are key drivers for revenue and technology inflections like backside power and GAA.
🔧 Upgrades and Installed Base Services Drive Recurring Revenue
Customer Support Business Group (CSBG) generated $1.7 billion, with record performance in upgrades. Upgrades were driven by technology migrations, particularly in DRAM and NAND. Lam’s ability to retrofit existing tools with next-gen capabilities—unique in the market—is increasingly valued by customers aiming to optimize capital efficiency.

🌐 Geographic Diversification and China Resilience
Lam derived 31% of total revenue from China, flat sequentially, with most sales to domestic Chinese firms. Taiwan and Korea each accounted for 24%, with Taiwan hitting a new record in dollar terms. Although export restrictions are in effect for some customers, Lam sees stable planning from remaining customers, and it continues to diversify its customer base globally.
🔍 Tariff Exposure Managed with Flexible Supply Chain
While monitoring the evolving tariff environment, Lam emphasized its global manufacturing footprint—including facilities in the U.S., Malaysia, Taiwan, Korea, and Austria—as a key mitigant. The company has not yet seen material changes to customer spending plans and expects minimal near-term financial disruption from tariff-related uncertainty.

🧠 Leadership in Simulation and Equipment Intelligence
Three new long-term agreements were signed for Lam’s virtual fabrication platform, Selera 3D, underscoring growing demand for AI-driven process simulation. Additionally, Lam is deploying intelligent services, cobots, and AI diagnostics to drive service revenue and support global fab ramp-ups with fewer skilled personnel on-site.
📦 Inventory and Capital Discipline in Growth Mode
Inventory rose slightly to $4.5 billion in anticipation of higher June-quarter shipments, with inventory turns at 2.2x. CapEx rose to $208 million, including land acquisition in India for R&D expansion. Lam repaid $500 million in debt and returned $643 million to shareholders through buybacks and dividends, maintaining strong capital discipline.

📊 Consistent Outlook Despite Macro and Tariff Headwinds
Lam reaffirmed its full-year WFE outlook in the $100 billion range, anticipating a first-half weighted revenue split. Management cited confidence in customer roadmaps and noted no signs of demand pull-ins or cancellations. China-related headwinds and Reliant tool shipment limits are factored into the forecast, with continued strength expected from Foundry and NAND.
📈 Path to Sustained Outperformance Against WFE Market
Building on recent Investor Day targets, Lam continues to expand its served available market (SAM), increase share through new product penetration in inflections like GAA and advanced packaging, and grow CSBG faster than its installed base. Management emphasized its confidence in sustained outperformance versus overall WFE growth through 2025 and beyond.

Micron Technology: Why I’m Buying the AI Memory Arms Dealer Before Wall Street Fully Wakes Up

A few weeks ago, Micron $MU looked unstoppable. Riding high on AI-fueled momentum, the stock was pushing $128 a breakout that seemed to signal a market finally pricing in the importance of high-bandwidth memory (HBM). But then, like clockwork, the tide turned.

First came a bearish note from Edgewater Research suggesting DRAM demand was losing steam and NAND was heading into a slump. A couple of days later, Goldman Sachs poured cold water with a neutral rating. The result? Micron shares slid nearly 11% from their June highs, settling near $114.

And yet I’m buying the dip.

Let me explain why. In this article, I’ll walk you through not just the short-term volatility, but the deeper, structural AI trends fueling Micron’s HBM growth. I’ll also dig into where the real opportunity lies, why I believe HBM4 will be a game-changer, and how Micron’s valuation is still well below where it should be for a company gearing up to dominate a crucial part of the AI supply chain.

The Panic Missed the Point: HBM Is the Story
Edgewater’s bearish take mostly revolved around traditional memory markets NAND and standard DRAM. Yes, NAND demand is sluggish. IDC cut its smartphone forecast again. AI PCs haven’t taken off as expected. And consumer demand? Still shaky. But here’s the nuance: NAND now makes up just 23% of Micron’s revenue, down from 30% a year ago. The real engine is DRAM and more specifically, HBM.

DRAM now accounts for over 76% of Micron’s total revenue. And that mix shift is no accident. It reflects a strategic pivot toward AI-related compute, where bandwidth and energy efficiency matter more than capacity alone.

So while the bears were fixated on smartphone softness, I was watching another data point: HBM3E inventory for 2025? Sold out. HBM4 sampling? Already underway. That’s the signal. And it’s loud.

HBM4: Micron’s Golden Ticket to the AI Future
If you're unfamiliar, HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) isn’t just a buzzword. It's the backbone of advanced AI workloads. It allows GPUs and custom ASICs to move massive volumes of data with ultra-low latency and far less power draw key for training and inference at hyperscale.

Micron is shipping HBM3E into $AMD’s MI350 accelerators and $NVDA Nvidia’s Blackwell chips. But the real breakthrough is HBM4, Micron’s 12-layer stack with 36GB capacity and 1-beta process technology, offering a 60% performance leap and 20% better power efficiency over HBM3E.

Let me be blunt: this isn’t vaporware. It's real product, with real customers, and a real moat.

What’s more, Micron confirmed that HBM4 production is locked and loaded for 2026. And demand? Already outpacing supply.

ASICs Enter the Chat: Dual Demand for HBM
The AI memory conversation isn’t just about GPUs anymore.

This month, TrendForce highlighted a coming surge in HBM demand from custom ASICs application-specific integrated circuits being developed by hyperscalers like Amazon, Meta, and Google. These players are no longer content to rely solely on Nvidia. They’re building their own AI chips—and they all want one thing: fast, efficient memory. Enter HBM.

Micron has already lined up at least two ASIC clients (the rumor mill points to Amazon and Broadcom), and HBM4’s customizability via logic-die tweaks makes it ideal for ASIC architectures.

Bottom line: we’re about to enter a phase of dual HBM demand GPUs and ASICs just as Micron ramps supply of its most competitive product yet.

Yes, Oversupply Is Coming But Not Yet
To be fair, HBM isn’t immune from cyclical risks. The $34 billion HBM market is attracting heavy competition from Samsung and SK Hynix. And yes, oversupply could hit in late 2026 or beyond.

But Micron isn’t trying to own the whole pie. Management is targeting a 23–24% market share aligned with its DRAM position and that’s a smart, sustainable approach. Unlike some rivals, Micron is scaling strategically, not blindly.

Where the Market Still Hasn’t Caught Up
Despite all of this, Micron trades like it’s a legacy memory play stuck in a cyclical rut. On a forward P/E basis, it’s just 15x far below the semiconductor sector average of ~24x. EV/EBITDA? Roughly 7.7x vs a peer median of 7x. Even the PEG ratio, which adjusts for growth, screams undervaluation at 0.3x well under the fair value threshold of 1x.

In other words, Wall Street hasn’t priced in Micron’s new identity: not just a memory supplier, but a critical enabler of the AI revolution.

Real Revenue Momentum
HBM revenue is already clocking in at a $6B+ annual run rate, growing at 50% quarter-over-quarter during the current ramp. All of 2025’s capacity? Gone. Most of 2026’s? Already allocated. And remember: HBM4 hasn’t even fully entered mass production yet.

As Sumit Sadana, Micron’s Chief Business Officer, said during the Q3 earnings call:

“We definitely look forward to the tailwind from that growth as well... we feel very good about the roadmap decisions that we've made relative to HBM4.”

That’s not just executive optimism it’s grounded in customer commitments and product specs.

Risks? Of Course. But Not Deal-Breakers
Let’s be clear: Micron operates in a cyclical, brutally competitive space. SK Hynix leads the HBM market for now, and Samsung is throwing money at the problem. Pricing pressure will come, and margin compression is always a risk.

But unlike past cycles, AI provides a structural tailwind. The rise of sovereign AI, energy-constrained datacenters, and custom chips all point to a future where memory isn’t just a commodity it’s a strategic advantage.

Final Take
We’re in the early innings of AI infrastructure buildout. Memory is the bottleneck, and HBM is the escape hatch. Micron is positioning itself not just as a follower, but as a formidable second mover with differentiated technology and a disciplined scaling plan.

At today’s price, the risk/reward is compelling. I believe the market is underestimating both the durability of AI memory demand and Micron’s ability to execute. For investors who can stomach the noise and look through the cycle, this is an opportunity to buy a foundational AI player at a non-AI valuation.

I’m long Micron. And I’m not waiting for the Street to catch up.

Growth
Micron’s growth story is defined by sharp turns, a cyclical giant now riding an AI-driven rebound. Over the past three years, revenue (-3.2% CAGR) and EPS have declined, reflecting tough industry conditions. post.text:
$AVGO $NVDA $GOOGL $AMZN TTN Research Alert: The Micron That Moves Markets: How CoWoP Could Unseat CoWoS in 2026 in The Quiet Power Shift Behind AI Packaging 

- CoWoS rules the AI-packaging roost in 2025 not because it is elegant, but because it is the only end-to-end industrialised route that hits all five constraints at once: HBM wiring density, power delivery, thermals, yield, and schedule. Foundry PDKs, OSAT playbooks, PI/SI sign-off, rework, and RMA machinery are all tuned to silicon-interposer CoWoS, so hyperscalers facing non-negotiable ship dates default to the path with the fewest unknowns. Even the notorious ABF-substrate bottleneck has been managed with allocations and incremental capacity, keeping the line moving for N5/N4/N3 GPUs hauling 6–8 stacks of HBM3E.

- Yet the ground is shifting. Early CoWoP tests are said to be strong enough that one R&D team has yanked its mass-production target forward to November 2025, a full year earlier than planned. CoWoP’s proposition is simple and subversive: delete the ABF package substrate, mount the chip plus silicon interposer straight onto a substrate-like PCB (SLP), and let panel economics, shorter verticals, and fewer defect-prone layers do the rest. If SLP can reliably print sub-10 μm line/space with tight impedance over large panels, CoWoP turns today’s packaging chokepoint into a throughput engine—reassigning bargaining power from ABF giants to SLP specialists in Taiwan and Korea.

- Alternatives exist but are not yet volume-worthy for top-bin accelerators. CoPoS (panel-level RDL) promises output and cost per area, but stable 8–15 μm fine lines at panel scale leave too little headroom for HBM4-era channels and power-integrity margins. Intel’s EMIB/Foveros family works—and ships—for platforms inside its ecosystem, but most of the current datacenter stack is TSMC logic plus HBM, where CoWoS is turnkey and thermally safer than stacking hot logic. OSAT “bridge” flows (FOCoS, SLIM) cut interposer area but still trail CoWoS in yield at very large body sizes. Fan-out variants shine at the edge, not yet in 700–1,000 W beasts.

- The technical swing factors for CoWoP are brutally specific. First, process window: SLP must achieve <10 μm L/S with AOI-clean yields and controlled impedance across full panels, not just coupons. Second, reliability: the ABF “mechanical buffer” vanishes, raising risks of package bow, micro-bump fatigue, and CAF in ultra-dense vias; JEDEC-style TC/THB/HTOL data must clear datacenter bars. Third, PDN closure: ultra-fine copper drives current density and EM to the brink; embedded-cap films, copper-coin rails, and fat-plane layering must hold IR-drop and transient response when a kilowatt package surges. If any leg wobbles, expect a limited NPI ramp in 4Q25 and broader volume sliding into 1H26—still a material pull-in versus the original 2026 plan.

- Economically, the first ten points of yield beat any notional BOM saving. CoWoP removes an expensive, yield-sapping ABF step and shortens cycle time; even if early SLP is dear, compounded yield can drop cost per accelerator by double digits at like-for-like HBM counts. The overlooked consequence is contract physics turned contract law: once panel formats and design rules harden, switching costs rise and de-facto standards emerge, shifting rent from concentrated ABF suppliers to a more fragmented—but newly pivotal—PCB universe. Cash-rich incumbents that pre-buy LDI/AOI capacity, copper foils, and mSAP chemistry will quietly lock in share before the rest of the market believes the curve.

- There are high-impact edge cases. Thinner stacks and dense via forests can couple acoustic energy into the board; under certain airflow regimes that can modulate jitter on marginal HBM channels, making chassis design a signal-integrity tool, not just a cooling problem. Shorter verticals move radiation planes, so early CoWoP servers risk EMI compliance surprises unless enclosure and optics are co-designed. Conversely, CoWoP’s panel DNA may permit localized PCB-side rework for non-die defects—an OPEX lever hyperscalers prize but most roadmaps ignore. And a pivot from ABF to SLP concentrates geopolitical risk differently: smart buyers will dual-source SLP by region to secure allocation during the next AI capex surge.

- The near-term playbook is pragmatic. CoWoS remains the production default through 2025 because it works. Bridge-hybrids that keep silicon where density is maximal and push everything else to panel/SLP will likely appear first, cushioning risk while bleeding in cost advantages. If CoWoP clears the three gates—fine-line yield, reliability, and PDN—by Q4 2025, a meaningful ramp is plausible, with volume scale in 1H26. If it misses by a micron—literally—expect a 3–6 month slip and continued scarcity pricing for ABF-centric flows. Either way, the strategic direction is set: the next cost/performance frontier in datacenter AI will be won not by another reticle-busting die, but by whoever industrialises HBM-grade panel packaging first and hardest.
(More at https://t.co/WjxSdE60bg)

The U.S. has revoked the Validated End User (VEU) status for TSMC, SK Hynix, and Samsung, effective December 31, 2025, ending their ability to easily export U.S. chipmaking equipment to their Chinese facilities. 

This move, part of the Trump administration’s push to limit China’s semiconductor advancements, requires these companies to obtain individual export licenses, potentially disrupting their operations in China. TSMC’s Nanjing plant, which accounts for less than 3% of its revenue, and SK Hynix and Samsung’s memory chip facilities will be affected, though the financial impact is expected to be minimal. 

The policy aims to curb China’s chip production capacity and technology transfer, while encouraging semiconductor manufacturing in the U.S. through incentives and tariff threats. 

However, it may benefit Chinese equipment makers and U.S. competitor Micron, while creating challenges for U.S. suppliers like Applied Materials and KLA Corp. South Korea and China have expressed concerns, with Seoul emphasizing the global supply chain’s stability and Beijing vowing to protect its enterprises.

🦔 AI data centers are creating a memory and storage shortage that could last a decade, with SSD and RAM prices already climbing fast. OpenAI's Stargate project alone has deals for 900,000 DRAM wafers monthly, representing 40% of global output, while Samsung's next-gen NAND is sold out before it even launches.

The Supply Chain Squeeze
Memory manufacturers learned from past boom-bust cycles and are deliberately constraining supply while redirecting capital to high-margin HBM production for AI rather than consumer products. Micron's entire 2026 HBM output is already committed, and every wafer devoted to AI is one not available for regular DRAM or NAND production.

Physical Constraints Hit Reality
Even if companies wanted to build more fabs, new facilities cost tens of billions and take years to produce at volume. Equipment suppliers like ASML face major backlogs, while China's rare earth restrictions complicate HDD production since hard drives are among the largest users of neodymium magnets globally.

Consumer Impact Already Visible
Raspberry Pi just raised prices by $5-10 due to memory costs rising 120% year-over-year. Western Digital's 2TB SSD went from $120 to $175, while DDR4 pricing is forecast to jump 38-43% quarter-over-quarter. The days of ultra-cheap storage upgrades are over.

My Take
This represents another physical constraint hitting AI scaling promises. While companies raise billions for AI infrastructure, the actual memory and storage components needed are becoming scarce and expensive. When basic building blocks like DRAM and NAND face decade-long shortages, it puts real limits on the data center expansion that AI valuations assume will continue indefinitely.

So @JonathanRoss321 keeps saying that NVIDIA is production constrained to 5M~ chips / year due to constrained HBM (high bandwidth memory) supply by SK Hynix / Samsung and CoWoS packaging capacity limitations by TSMC... I decided to do an extra deep fact check on this ... NO LIES! Conclusion: @GroqInc is extremely undervalued.

NVIDIA Supply Constraints: HBM and CoWoS

- Confirmed: NVIDIA faces significant production bottlenecks due to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) supply from suppliers like SK Hynix and Samsung, and TSMC's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity. Sources (e.g., NVIDIA Q3 FY25 earnings, analyst reports from Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan) indicate CoWoS limits output. TSMC's CoWoS capacity is 35K–40K wafers/month in 2024, expanding to 65K–75K/month in 2025. NVIDIA secures ~50–60% of this, equating to ~35K–45K wafers/month by end-2025. Assuming 4–8 AI GPUs per CoWoS wafer (based on die size for H100/Blackwell), this supports ~3–4M units/year in 2024, ramping to ~5–6M in 2025. HBM shortages further cap this, with nearly all 2025 Blackwell production reportedly pre-sold.

Groq Supply Constraints

- Confirmed Not Constrained in Same Way: Groq's Language Processing Unit (LPU) avoids HBM, using on-chip SRAM instead, eliminating dependency on scarce HBM. It manufactures at GlobalFoundries on 14nm node, which has excess capacity compared to TSMC's 4nm/5nm used by NVIDIA. Groq describes its supply chain as "commodity" (Jonathan Ross quotes), allowing much faster scaling without 12–18 month lead times for GPUs.

memory semi conduct Q&A key takeaway

Q. Why has demand for conventional DRAM suddenly increased in just one month?
A. First, the primary reason is that the focus on AI servers over the past two years has limited investment in CPU-based general servers, resulting in a lower base of demand. Another factor is the shift in architecture for AI workload processing, leading to the co-existence of GPU-based AI servers and CPU-based general servers. As AI models become more sophisticated and expert models become the norm, CPU servers are handling all the processing, including distributing AI workloads to each expert and collating the computational results, reducing the load on GPU servers. Demand for HBM in GPU servers continues to grow, while demand for conventional DRAM in CPU servers is also increasing. This simultaneous increase in demand for DRAM, such as SOCAM and GDDR7, which were not previously used in servers, is exacerbating the overall capacity shortage.

Q. Why do you anticipate a prolonged supply shortage?
A. The focus on HBM over the past two years has limited investment in conventional DRAM. Greenfield investments in 2026 include Samsung Electronics' P4 East Side and SK Hynix's M15x Phase 1, both for HBM4. Future greenfield investments include Samsung Electronics' PS and SK Hynix's Yongin Y1, both of which are expected to contribute capacity after the second half of 2027. Until then, conventional DRAM must meet upside demand primarily through process migration within limited cleanroom capacity. Therefore, a severe shortage is expected during the current period of rapidly increasing demand. Furthermore, a significant increase in HBM content is expected in 2027 compared to 2026. This is due to the launch of NVIDIA's Rubin Ultra and the full-scale production of new products with increased HBM adoption by major ASIC companies. Given the current AI workload trend, where AI servers and general servers are growing simultaneously, the simultaneous growth in demand for HBM and server-oriented conventional DRAM is expected to be prolonged, and the DRAM supply shortage will inevitably persist until new capacity is added in the second half of 2027. 

Q. What is your outlook for HBM prices in 2026?
A. We believe a price decline for HBM3e is inevitable. As mentioned in previous notes, this is primarily due to the natural elimination of the price premium following the launch of the new HBM4 product, rather than intensifying competition. We believe HBM4 can see further price increases compared to previously discussed prices. NVIDIA's increased speed requirements will negatively impact yields and margins for suppliers, so there will likely be a push to pass this on to suppliers. Especially with the overall DRAM supply shortage exacerbated by conventional DRAM, if HBM does not secure sufficient margins, memory suppliers will have little incentive to actively produce HBM. Just as Micron has already shifted some of its 2026 HBM plans to server DRAM, if the margin gap between HBM and conventional DRAM narrows, memory customers will likely prioritize customers with higher margins. The DRAM supply shortage will strengthen memory suppliers' negotiating power with customers.

AI Semiconductors = More Materials, Larger Packages, Higher Demand

Compared with conventional chips, AI semiconductors require larger packages and more components. This shift is driving a surge in demand for advanced semiconductor materials.

🔹 Conventional semiconductors rely on:
•Epoxy molding compounds (EMC) – #2 global market share
•Solder resist – Global top class
•Copper clad laminates (CCL) – #1 global market share

🔹 AI semiconductors demand even more specialized materials:
•Insulating adhesive films (HBM) – Global top class
•Thermal interface materials (TIM, sheet type) – Global top class
•Photosensitive insulation materials (PID) – #1 global market share
•Liquid underfill – #2 global market share

Resonac is investing aggressively:
By 2027, capacity is planned to expand 3.5x to 5x the 2023 level (~¥16B CAPEX).

As AI accelerates, backend packaging materials are no longer “hidden enablers” — they are strategic growth drivers shaping the semiconductor supply chain.
